1942.history: Capcom's 1942 hit arcades in 1984 as a vertical World War II shoot-em-up, sending a lone fighter up Pacific island screens against endless enemy planes. Home ports followed across the mid-1980s on systems including the Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and other micros, bringing a major Japanese arcade brand into European living rooms. Its looping stages, power-ups and high-score chase helped define the vertical shmup template that later Amiga and ST shooters still echoed.

221B Baker Street.history: Datasoft brought the Sherlock Holmes board game 221B Baker Street to home computers around 1986, with versions for the Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST and other platforms. Players move between London locations, gather clues and race to solve cases before rivals do. As a licensed deduction title rather than a pure arcade conversion, it stood out on 8- and 16-bit machines for turning tabletop mystery logic into a competitive computer party game.

5th Gear.history: 5th Gear is a top-down driving combat game by Fantastic Four, published by Hewson on the Rack-It budget label. The Commodore 64 original appeared in 1988, with Atari ST and Amiga ports following around 1989–1990. You steer a car through maze-like wilderness courses, shooting rival vehicles and spending earned cash on upgrades. It never became a flagship Hewson title, but it was a typical late-80s budget action release bridging 8-bit and 16-bit catalogues.

A Pig Quest.history: A Pig Quest is a modern Commodore 64 homebrew action-adventure platformer released in 2023 by the Piggy 18 Team and published by Protovision on a high-capacity cartridge. Across five large worlds, players explore, fight and solve light puzzles as an unlikely porcine hero. With detailed bitmap art and a large dynamic SID score, it became one of the most acclaimed contemporary C64 releases, showing how far new commercial software on the machine can still go.

A Prehistoric Tale.history: A Prehistoric Tale is a cute platform-puzzle game developed by The Lost Boys and published by Thalion Software for the Amiga and Atari ST in 1990. Inspired by the Commodore 64 classic Dino Eggs, it tasks players with rescuing dinosaur eggs across dozens of screens, including a cooperative two-player mode. It is remembered as a polished Thalion curiosity and as an early commercial credit for ST demo-scene talent who later moved into bigger industry roles.

Ace II.history: ACE 2 (Air Combat Emulator 2), published by Cascade Games in 1987, is an arcade-leaning combat flight sequel to ACE for the Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and other formats. It simplified flight controls and leaned hard into split-screen dogfighting, letting two players duel head-to-head. On 8-bit machines it mattered less as a serious sim than as an accessible two-player flyer in Cascade's mid-price line-up.

After Burner.history: Sega's After Burner stormed arcades in 1987 with afterburning jets, dramatic scaling and sit-down cabinets. Home computer ports by Activision and others arrived soon after on Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, CPC and more. Though the micros could not match the arcade hardware, the conversions still sold the fantasy of high-speed aerial combat and became a familiar late-80s showcase of how far 16-bit machines could push pseudo-3D action.

Agent X II.history: Agent X II: The Mad Prof's Back is a 1987 Mastertronic budget title for Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum. The sequel stitches three genres together—side-scrolling shooter, platform infiltration and a Breakout-style finale—into one cheap cassette adventure. It is best remembered on the C64 for Tim Follin's soundtrack, which outshone the uneven multi-style gameplay and helped the game linger in SID music collections.

Agony.history: Agony is a horizontally scrolling fantasy shoot-em-up developed by Art & Magic and published by Psygnosis for the Amiga in 1992. Players guide a magical owl through richly drawn stages filled with bosses and power-ups. Famous as much for Chris Hülsbeck's soundtrack as for its graphics, it became a late OCS Amiga showcase and a staple of Psygnosis's glossy European action catalogue.

Airborne Ranger.history: MicroProse released Airborne Ranger in 1987 as a tactical action game about a lone U.S. Army Ranger dropped behind enemy lines. Versions appeared on Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST and other platforms. Mixing stealth, timed objectives and open maps, it stood apart from pure arcade shooters and helped prove that MicroProse's military sims could work as tense, mission-based action on home computers.

Airwolf II.history: Airwolf II is Elite Systems' 1987 side-scrolling helicopter shooter, a loose sequel to its earlier Airwolf TV tie-in for Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and related machines. Distant from the show's plots, it sends the chopper through alien-invasion stages collecting weapons. As a budget-friendly Elite shooter it kept the Airwolf brand alive on 8-bit shelves after the first game's success.

Alien Breed.history: Team17's Alien Breed launched on the Amiga in 1991 as a top-down sci-fi run-and-gun clearly inspired by Aliens and Gauntlet. One or two players blast through corridor complexes packed with aliens, keys and weapon pickups. Its arcade intensity, co-op play and later expansions made it one of the defining early Team17 hits and a cornerstone of early-90s Amiga action gaming.

Alien Breed II.history: Alien Breed II: The Horror Continues arrived on the Amiga in 1993 as Team17's bigger, meaner follow-up to the original corridor shooter. It expanded maps, weapons and enemy variety while keeping the frantic co-op blast-athons that fans wanted. On AGA and OCS Amigas it reinforced Alien Breed as a house franchise and kept Team17 near the top of the European action charts.

Alien Breed: Tower Assault.history: Alien Breed: Tower Assault, released by Team17 in 1994 for Amiga computers and CD32, pushes the series into a tower-assault campaign with branching routes and denser firefights. Still a top-down co-op shooter, it polished the formula for mid-90s hardware and CD distribution. It stands as one of the last major classic-era Alien Breed releases before the series moved on from the Amiga.

Aliens.history: Electric Dreams' Aliens (1986) adapted the film for home computers, with notable versions on Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum. Rather than a simple platformer, it mixes tense base exploration, motion-tracker dread and squad management vibes from the movie. On the C64 especially it became one of the stronger mid-80s film licences, remembered for atmosphere more than arcade flash.

Altered Beast.history: Sega's Altered Beast began in the arcades in 1988 as a side-scrolling beat-em-up in which a resurrected warrior transforms into beasts. Activision and others brought it to Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and CPC soon after. Home ports varied in quality, but the game still mattered as a high-profile Sega conversion that put arcade transformation combat onto European 16-bit machines.

Ambermoon.history: Ambermoon is Thalion Software's 1993 Amiga role-playing epic, the sequel to Amberstar and the deeper second half of designer Karsten Köper's trilogy plans. It offers a vast fantasy world, first-person towns and dungeons, and complex party adventuring on late Amiga hardware. Long admired by RPG fans, it is often cited as one of the Amiga's most ambitious German-designed computer role-playing games.

Amberstar.history: Amberstar, published by Thalion in 1992 for Amiga, Atari ST and DOS, opens Karsten Köper's epic fantasy RPG cycle. Players assemble a party and explore a large world through a mix of 2D overworld travel and character-driven questing. As a flagship German RPG on 16-bit computers, it built the foundation later continued—and surpassed in scope—by Ambermoon on the Amiga.

Anarchy.history: Anarchy is a 1990 Psygnosis puzzle game developed by The Assembly Line for Amiga and Atari ST. Players clear cascading block layouts with a laser in tightly designed, abstract stages. Coming from the team behind Xenon 2's publisher era puzzle experiments, it showed Psygnosis branching beyond shooters into brain-teasing action and remains a cult entry in their early-90s catalogue.

Another World.history: Éric Chahi's Another World (known as Out of This World in North America) was released by Delphine Software in 1991, with the Amiga version especially celebrated. Its rotoscoped animation, cinematic storytelling and lethal puzzle-platform challenges made it feel closer to an interactive movie than a typical European platformer. It became a landmark Amiga showcase and influenced cinematic action-adventure design for years.

Apidya.history: Apidya is a 1992 Amiga horizontal shoot-em-up by Kaiko, published by Eclipse. Players control an insect warrior through lush, organic stages packed with inventive enemies and bosses. Widely praised for polish and for Chris Hülsbeck's soundtrack, it ranks among the Amiga's finest original shmups and a high-water mark for German action development on the platform.

Apprentice.history: Apprentice is a colourful side-scrolling platformer released by Rainbow Arts around 1990 for Amiga and Atari ST. As a young magician, you kick boxes, shop for extras and battle through elemental stages toward a dragon confrontation. Cutesy and console-like in tone, it fitted Rainbow Arts' family-friendly action line and gave 16-bit owners a breezy alternative to grimmer European platformers.

Archon: The Light and the Dark.history: Archon: The Light and the Dark, created by Free Fall Associates and published by Electronic Arts in 1983, blends chess-like strategy with real-time arcade combats when pieces clash. Iconic on the Commodore 64 and later ported to Amiga, Atari and other systems, it proved EA's early computer catalogue could fuse board-game depth with action. It remains one of the defining hybrid strategy games of the 8-bit era.

Arkanoid.history: Taito's Arkanoid updated Breakout for 1986 arcades with capsules, power-ups and the cute enemy presence of Doh's world. Home conversions flooded European computers—Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, CPC and more—becoming a defining bat-and-ball craze. On micros it mattered as both a faithful arcade port and a template for countless brick-breaking clones.

Arkanoid II: Revenge of Doh.history: Arkanoid II: Revenge of Doh continues Taito's brick-breaker formula with tougher layouts and new power-ups after the arcade original's success. Home versions reached Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and other platforms in the late 1980s. For computer owners it extended the Arkanoid boom, giving players a tougher sequel once they had cleared the first game's Vaus-and-bricks loop.

Arkanoid: Revenge of Doh.history: Arkanoid: Revenge of Doh is Taito's arcade sequel to Arkanoid, widely converted to late-80s home computers including Amiga, Atari ST and Commodore 64. It keeps the Vaus paddle-and-ball core while adding new capsules, enemies and demanding patterns. On European micros it was the standard second dose of Arkanoid fever after the first game's massive port wave.

Armalyte.history: Armalyte, developed by Cyberdyne Systems and published by Thalamus in 1988, is a horizontally scrolling shoot-em-up celebrated as one of the Commodore 64's finest. Smooth scrolling, fierce difficulty and polished presentation made it a technical and gameplay showcase for the machine. It became a touchstone C64 shmup and a highlight of Thalamus's quality-focused late-80s line-up.

Artura.history: Artura is a late-1980s Arthurian action-adventure platformer published by Gremlin Graphics for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, CPC and Spectrum. Players explore castle environments, fight enemies and pursue a loosely mythical quest as a young warrior. Reviews were mixed, but it remains a typical Gremlin 8-/16-bit cross-format release from the peak licence-and-legend era.

Asphalt.history: Asphalt is a 1987 top-down vehicular combat game published by Ubisoft (often associated with French microcomputer development) for platforms including the Amstrad CPC. You ride a heavily armed truck along hostile highways, managing weapons and damage while blasting rival vehicles. It reflects the French CPC scene's taste for stylish action concepts beyond simple British platform clones.

Atari Arcade Classics.history: Atari Arcade Classics is a compilation pack of early Atari coin-op hits—typically including titles such as Battlezone, Crystal Castles, Missile Command and Super Breakout—bundled for the Atari ST, notably with hardware packs like the STart Pack. It packaged foundational arcade history onto disk for 16-bit Atari owners, serving more as a heritage bundle than a new original game.

Auf Wiedersehen Monty.history: Auf Wiedersehen Monty is Gremlin Graphics' 1987 sequel to the Monty Mole platform adventures, released for Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and related machines. Monty tours Europe through flick-screen levels packed with jokes, hazards and collectibles. It capped a beloved British platform comedy series and remains a high point of Gremlin's 8-bit character platformers.

B.A.T..history: B.A.T. (Bureau of Astral Troubleshooters), released by Ubisoft around 1990 for Amiga, Atari ST and other computers, is a cyberpunk adventure blending investigation, dialogue and occasional action. Set in a dense futuristic city, it stood out for atmosphere and systems-heavy design rather than pure arcade reflexes. On 16-bit machines it helped establish Ubisoft's early reputation for ambitious European adventures.

Baal.history: Baal is a dark platform shoot-em-up released in 1988 under Psygnosis's Psyclapse label for Amiga, Atari ST and later other formats. As a Time Warrior you explore hellish domains, fight demons and recover pieces of a stolen war machine. With glossy presentation and labyrinthine stages, it fitted Psygnosis's early branded look and gave 16-bit owners a moody alternative to brighter platformers.

Backlash.history: Backlash is a fast first-person 3D shoot-em-up by Novagen Software, created by Paul Woakes and released around 1987–1988 for Atari ST and Amiga. In the spirit of Battlezone-style tank combat, it emphasises smooth motion and arcade reflexes over simulation. Coming from the maker of Encounter and Mercenary, it was a showcase of Novagen's talent for convincing 3D action on 16-bit Ataris and Amigas.

Bad Dudes vs. DragonNinja.history: Data East's Bad Dudes vs. DragonNinja (arcade, 1988) is a side-scrolling beat-em-up about rescuing the U.S. President from ninjas. Ocean Software brought home versions to Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, CPC and other platforms. On European computers it joined Ocean's wave of coin-op conversions, delivering co-op brawling that mirrored the arcade's tongue-in-cheek American action tone.

Bangkok Knights.history: Bangkok Knights is a Muay Thai fighting game from System 3, first released on Commodore 64 in 1987 and later ported to Amiga and Atari ST. Large character sprites and one-on-one bouts through Thai venues made it stand out among late-80s martial-arts titles. On the C64 it is also remembered for Rob Hubbard's music, which boosted its profile beyond the fighting mechanics alone.

Banshee.history: Banshee is a 1994 vertical shoot-em-up by Core Design for AGA Amiga 1200 and CD32. It pairs slick scrolling and huge bosses with a distinctive alternate-world aesthetic and destructible detail. Released late in the Amiga's commercial life, it is widely regarded as one of the platform's best original shmups and a technical farewell flourish for Core's action work.

Barbarian.history: Palace Software's Barbarian: The Ultimate Warrior (1987) is a one-on-one sword-fighting game infamous for its brutal finishing moves and Maria Whittaker box art. Versions spread across Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST, CPC and more. On home computers it became a cultural talking point as much as a fighter, defining Palace's provocative marketing and the late-80s versus combat craze.

Batman.history: Ocean Software's Batman (1989), tied to Tim Burton's film, brought the Dark Knight to Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and other platforms through action stages inspired by the movie's look. As one of Ocean's major late-80s licences, it showed how film tie-ins could be more than rushed platform clones. It helped cement Batman as a recurring prestige property on European home computers.

Batman: The Caped Crusader.history: Batman: The Caped Crusader (1988) is Ocean's comic-inspired adventure for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and related machines. Players tackle cases in a distinctive comic-panel presentation mixing investigation and action sequences. Released before the Burton film wave, it gave 8- and 16-bit owners a stylish Batman game rooted in the comic-book identity rather than a single movie licence.

Batman: The Movie.history: Batman: The Movie (1989) is Ocean's official home-computer adaptation of Tim Burton's film, released on Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, CPC and other formats. Stages recreate key film set-pieces with platforming and action challenges dressed in the movie's gothic style. It was one of Ocean's blockbuster licences of the era and a defining Batman release on European micros.

Battle Squadron.history: Battle Squadron is a 1989 Amiga vertical shoot-em-up by Instinct Design, published by Innerprise, later appearing on other platforms. Known for intense bullet patterns, co-op play and strong presentation, it became a favourite among Amiga shmup fans. Its full title often references the Destruction of the Barrax Empire storyline that frames the campaign.

Battle Squadron: The Destruction of the.history: Battle Squadron: The Destruction of the Barrax Empire is the full title of Instinct Design's late-1980s Amiga vertical shooter published by Innerprise. One or two players fight through relentless alien assault waves in a campaign against the Barrax Empire. Highly regarded for speed and challenge, it ranks among the Amiga's essential original shoot-em-ups of the OCS era.

Battle Valley.history: Battle Valley is a side-scrolling military shoot-em-up published by Hewson around 1988–1989 for Commodore 64, Amiga and Amstrad CPC. Players switch between helicopter and tank to destroy terrorist bases and recover stolen nuclear weapons under a tight time limit. The dual-vehicle design made it distinctive among Hewson action titles and earned strong praise especially on the C64.

Battletech - The Crescent Hawk's Incepti.history: BattleTech: The Crescent Hawk's Inception (1988), developed with Westwood Associates and published via Infocom/Activision, is a MechWarrior-style RPG/strategy adventure on platforms including Commodore 64 and Amiga. Players train, deploy BattleMechs and pursue a story of inheritance and intrigue in FASA's BattleTech universe. It brought tabletop mech lore to home computers before larger BattleTech games arrived.

Beneath a Steel Sky.history: Beneath a Steel Sky is a 1994 cyberpunk point-and-click adventure by Revolution Software, published by Virgin, with art by comics legend Dave Gibbons. Originally released on PC and Amiga, it follows outsider Robert Foster through a dystopian city using Revolution's Virtual Theatre system. It stands as one of the Amiga's great graphic adventures and a landmark British adventure-game release.

Beneath a Steel Sky (CD32).history: The Amiga CD32 edition of Beneath a Steel Sky brings Revolution Software's 1994 dystopian adventure to Commodore's CD console, benefiting from CD storage for the full point-and-click experience. Like other versions, it features Dave Gibbons' visual design and Virtual Theatre character routines. For CD32 owners it was a flagship adventure that showed the machine could host major European narrative games.

Benefactor.history: Benefactor is a 1994 Amiga and CD32 puzzle-platformer developed by Digital Illusions CE (DICE) and published by Psygnosis. Tiny hero Ben E. Factor rescues and guides Merry Men through intricate levels that blend platform skill with Lemmings-like planning. Coming late in the Amiga era, it showcased Swedish talent under the Psygnosis banner and remains a cult favourite for its clever stage design.

Beverly Hills Cop.history: Beverly Hills Cop is a late-1980s/early-1990s film licence game published by Tynesoft for platforms including Amiga, Atari ST and Commodore 64. It translates Eddie Murphy's buddy-cop movie into multi-load action sections typical of the era's tie-ins. Never a critical darling, it still illustrates how Hollywood brands filled European computer charts alongside original hits.

Beyond the Ice Palace.history: Beyond the Ice Palace is a side-scrolling action platformer published by Elite Systems in 1988 for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum. Players fight through fantasy stages with weapon throws and branching routes toward a dark citadel. As a cross-format Elite release it was part of the late-80s push to give 8- and 16-bit owners arcade-style fantasy combat.

Bionic Commando.history: Capcom's Bionic Commando began in arcades in 1987, famous for its swinging grappling-arm mechanic instead of jumping. Home ports and related versions reached Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and later 16-bit machines. On European micros the arm-swinging combat made it one of Capcom's most distinctive conversions and a favourite among platform-shooter fans.

Bitmap Brothers' Magic Pockets.history: Magic Pockets (1991) is a Bitmap Brothers platformer published with Renegade, starring the Bitmaps' own 'Bitmap Kid' who stores weapons and gadgets in magical pockets. Released on Amiga and Atari ST, it applied the team's stylish presentation to a more whimsical genre than Speedball or Xenon. It remains a cult Bitmap Brothers title from their early-90s commercial peak.

Black Lamp.history: Black Lamp is a 1988 fantasy platform-adventure published by Firebird for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and other formats. You play a jester collecting lamps through castle rooms while dodging creatures and hazards. Light-hearted but tricky, it was a typical late-80s UK microcomputer platformer and a recurring entry in Firebird's broad budget-to-midrange catalogue.

Blood Money.history: Blood Money is a 1989 horizontal shoot-em-up by DMA Design, published by Psygnosis for Amiga, Atari ST and other systems. Players buy weapons between stages and blast through varied planetary environments in one of DMA's early commercial hits. Polished and demanding, it helped establish DMA's reputation before Lemmings and fitted Psygnosis's flashy Amiga action brand.

BMX Simulator.history: BMX Simulator, created by the Oliver Twins and published by Codemasters in 1986, is a top-down BMX racing game that began on platforms such as the Amstrad CPC and Commodore 64 before spreading widely. Multiple camera views, tracks and two-player races made it a budget sports staple. It helped define Codemasters' simulator brand and the Oliver Twins' early success on 8-bit machines.

Bob Winner.history: Bob Winner is a mid-1980s French action-adventure by Loriciels, released on Amstrad CPC, Commodore 64, Atari ST and related machines. The hero competes through varied challenges to obtain keys and uncover a lost civilisation. Typical of Loriciels' CPC-era output, it brought a distinctly French multi-event style to European microcomputer shelves.

Bomb Jack.history: Tehkan's (Tecmo) Bomb Jack leapt from 1984 arcades into European homes via Elite Systems ports on Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and later other formats. Players collect bombs on single-screen platforms while avoiding enemies, using a powerful jump. It became one of the most recognisable early arcade conversions on UK micros and a staple of Elite's coin-op line.

Bomberland.history: Bomberland is a modern Commodore 64 homebrew Bomberman-style maze action game released on cartridge by RGCD in 2013. Developed over years by Michal Okowicki with music by Owen Crowley, it offers a lengthy single-player campaign plus multiplayer for several players with supported adapters. It is a standout of the 2010s C64 homebrew revival rather than a 1980s commercial original.

Bombo.history: Bombo is a mid-1980s Commodore 64 platform action game published in the UK budget market (Entertainment USA / related labels), often compared to Bomb Jack-style collect-and-avoid play. You hop through single-screen stages grabbing items while dodging foes. As a cheap cassette-era title it was part of the C64's flood of arcade-inspired platformers rather than a major franchise landmark.

Bonanza Bros..history: Sega's Bonanza Bros. debuted in arcades in 1990 as a co-op heist action game about two thieves infiltrating buildings. Home ports followed on Amiga, Atari ST and other systems in the early 1990s. On 16-bit computers it stood out for dual-character comedy stealth-action, giving European Amiga and ST owners another distinctive Sega conversion beyond pure beat-em-ups.

Boulder Dash.history: Boulder Dash arrived in 1984 from First Star Software, created by Peter Liepa and Chris Gray. On the Commodore 64 it became a defining puzzle-action hit: guide Rockford through caves, dig dirt, dodge falling boulders and butterflies, and collect diamonds under a ticking clock. Tight physics and level design made every screen a miniature puzzle. Ports followed across Amstrad CPC, Atari 8-bit, and later 16-bit machines, but the C64 original cemented the series’ reputation and inspired countless diggers and clone caves throughout the 1980s.

Boulder Dash II: Rockford's Revenge.history: Boulder Dash II: Rockford's Revenge followed in 1985 from First Star Software as a full new set of caves for the diamond-hunting formula. Rockford still digs, pushes rocks, and races the timer, but the layouts push trickier timing and enemy patterns. On the Commodore 64 and other home systems it proved the first game was no one-off, extending a puzzle-action template that European magazines and players kept citing for years. It kept the series visible while clones and later Boulder Dash variants filled budget racks.

Bounder.history: Bounder is a 1985 bouncing-ball platformer from Gremlin Graphics, best known on the Commodore 64 and ZX Spectrum and later seen on Amstrad CPC and other micros. You control a tennis-ball-like hero hopping across floating platforms, collecting points and surviving awkward leaps more than combat. Its breezy presentation and score-chasing levels made it a typical mid-80s UK arcade-style original. On 8-bit machines it stood out as a light, addictive alternative to shooters and licensed film games of the same year.

Briley Witch Chronicles.history: Briley Witch Chronicles is a modern homebrew Japanese-inspired RPG for the Commodore 64, released in 2021 by Sarah Jane Avory (Witchsoft). Built for EasyFlash cartridge hardware, it offers a long story-driven adventure with exploration, dialogue, potion crafting, and turn-based combat—including a talking cat companion. Unlike 1980s C64 RPGs constrained by tape and disk limits, it uses contemporary cartridge capacity for fuller maps and presentation. It became a showcase of what new C64 development can still deliver decades after the machine’s commercial era.

Bruce Lee.history: Bruce Lee, published by Datasoft in 1984 and designed by Ron Fortier, mixed platforming with martial-arts brawling across a multi-screen fortress. Players fight ninja and a sumo warrior while collecting lanterns and navigating traps. On the Commodore 64—and in strong Atari and other home ports—it was one of the early licensed martial-arts hits that felt like an arcade-style action game rather than a pure fighting sim. Its compact rooms, two-player modes on some versions, and memorable difficulty made it a staple of mid-80s 8-bit libraries.

Bruce Lee II.history: Bruce Lee II is a modern unofficial homebrew sequel, first made for PC by Bruno R. Marcos in 2013 and ported to the Commodore 64 by Jonas Hultén in 2015. It revives the 1984 Datasoft formula of platforming, lantern collecting, and hand-to-hand combat against ninja foes across new fortress screens. Explicitly a fan project rather than a 1980s commercial release, the C64 version pushed the hardware with disk and EasyFlash builds. It shows how classic 8-bit action templates still attract new development in the homebrew scene.

Bubble Bobble.history: Bubble Bobble began as a 1986 Taito arcade co-op classic by Fukio Mitsuji: dinosaurs Bub and Bob trap enemies in bubbles, then burst them for fruit and power-ups across hundreds of single-screen levels. Home ports landed on Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, Atari ST, Amiga, and more, bringing the cute-but-fiendish platformer to living rooms. On European micros it was prized for faithful two-player fun and escalating stage gimmicks. The conversion wave helped make Taito’s bubble-blowing formula one of the most widely played arcade experiences of the late 1980s.

Buck Rogers: Countdown to Doomsday.history: Buck Rogers: Countdown to Doomsday is a 1990 science-fiction RPG from Strategic Simulations, Inc., built on the Gold Box engine used for SSI’s AD&D titles. Set in the Buck Rogers XXVC universe, it offers party-based exploration, tactical combat, and a campaign against the Russo-American Mercantile. Versions for Amiga, Commodore 64, and other platforms brought SSI’s computer RPG style into a licensed pulp-future setting. For Amiga and C64 owners it sat alongside the Krynn and Forgotten Realms Gold Box games as another deep, turn-based adventure from the peak SSI era.

Bumpy's Arcade Fantasy.history: Bumpy's Arcade Fantasy is a 1992 puzzle-platformer from French publisher Loriciel, released for Amiga, Atari ST, Amstrad CPC, and PC. You steer Bumpy, a bouncing ball character, through more than a hundred screens of platforms, traps, and collectibles arranged as themed arcade attractions. Timing jumps and reading moving hazards matter more than shooting. On 16-bit machines it fit the European taste for colorful skill-and-puzzle hybrids, offering a long, increasingly cruel challenge that rewarded precision rather than arcade reflex alone.

Burnin' Rubber.history: Burnin' Rubber is a 1990 arcade-style racing game by Ocean Software, bundled on cartridge with Amstrad’s CPC+ computers and the GX4000 console. Inspired by endurance racing and Ocean’s earlier WEC Le Mans work, it uses a behind-the-car view across timed laps with day-night progression. As one of the few prominent titles built for Amstrad’s enhanced Plus hardware, it became the pack-in showcase for the short-lived CPC+/GX4000 range. For CPC collectors it remains a signature cartridge race rather than a multi-format chart staple.

Cabal.history: Cabal started as a late-1980s TAD Corporation arcade shooter and reached home computers through Ocean and other publishers around 1989–1990. Players man a lone soldier against waves of enemies, aiming with a crosshair while limited movement and cover keep the action tense—part Operation Wolf cousin, part stage-clearing run-and-gun. Ports for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, and others brought the cabinet’s destructive set pieces to micros. On those machines it stood out among light-gun-style conversions for its chunky sprites and relentless enemy density.

Cadaver.history: Cadaver is a 1990 isometric action-adventure from The Bitmap Brothers, published by Image Works. You play the thief Karadoc exploring the haunted Castle Wulf, solving object puzzles, fighting creatures, and mapping multi-level rooms in a blend of arcade immediacy and adventure logic. On Amiga and Atari ST it showcased the Brothers’ polished 16-bit presentation after Speedball and Xenon 2. Critics praised its atmosphere and interaction depth, helping prove isometric dungeon crawls could feel modern on European home computers.

Cadaver: The Payoff.history: Cadaver: The Payoff (1991) is the data-disk continuation of The Bitmap Brothers’ isometric adventure Cadaver, again aimed at Amiga and Atari ST players. It extends Karadoc’s story with a new castle campaign, fresh puzzles, and the same object-driven exploration and combat. Released when expansion disks were a common way to deepen 16-bit hits, it rewarded owners who wanted more of Wulf’s trap-filled rooms without waiting for a full sequel. Together with the original, it rounded out one of the Bitmap Brothers’ most adventure-leaning efforts.

Cannon Fodder.history: Cannon Fodder, released in 1993 by Sensible Software and Virgin, is a darkly comic real-time tactics shooter. Tiny soldiers scramble across isometric warzones while the game tracks named recruits and a grim home-front memorial. Controls are simple—point, shoot, throw grenades—but missions punish careless losses. On Amiga especially it became a defining early-90s hit, sparking controversy over its poppy tone and anti-war sting while proving Sensible could match their soccer fame with a sharp action strategy classic later ported widely.

Cannon Fodder (AGA).history: Cannon Fodder (AGA) is the Amiga 1200/4000 enhanced edition of Sensible Software’s 1993 real-time war game. It keeps the isometric squad missions, named soldiers, and bleak humor of the original while taking advantage of AGA machines’ extra colors and smoother presentation where supported. For many Amiga owners in the mid-1990s this was the preferred way to play the Virgin-published classic as OCS/ECS hardware aged. Gameplay remains the same pointed satire of disposable infantry that made the series famous on 16-bit systems.

Cannon Fodder 2.history: Cannon Fodder 2 followed in 1994 from Sensible Software, again published by Virgin. It expands the real-time squad action with new theaters, tougher mission design, and the same roll-call of fragile recruits. Amiga players got another round of pinpoint shooting, jeep and vehicle set pieces, and the series’ trademark mix of catchy presentation and fatal consequences. While some preferred the tighter original campaign, the sequel kept Sensible’s war satire current on 16-bit machines just as PC and console ports broadened the audience.

Captain Blood.history: Captain Blood (French: L'Arche du Captain Blood) is a 1988 cinematic space adventure from Exxos/ERE Informatique, designed by Philippe Ulrich and others with distinctive art by Didier Bouchon. You pilot the ship Ark seeking cloned duplicates across alien worlds, communicating through an iconic icon-based alien language rather than text menus. Amiga, Atari ST, and other versions made it a flagship of late-80s French “new wave” design—strange, stylish, and atmospheric. On 16-bit computers it stood apart from conventional space traders and shooters.

Captive.history: Captive is a 1990 science-fiction dungeon crawler by Tony Crowther, published by Mindscape for Amiga, Atari ST, and other systems. Trapped in a space prison, you remote-control a squad of droids through multi-level bases, combining first-person exploration, combat, and gadget management. Its look and feel invited comparisons to Dungeon Master in a tech setting. On Amiga especially it earned a strong following for depth and atmosphere, later spawning the related PC title Liberation, and it remains a high point of Crowther’s 16-bit design work.

Carrier Command.history: Carrier Command, released in 1988 by Realtime Games and Rainbird, blends real-time strategy with vehicle action around a futuristic aircraft carrier. Players capture island chains by launching fighters, amphibious craft, and drones while managing resources and repairing damage. Amiga and Atari ST versions were showpieces of late-80s 3D ambition, with a Commodore 64 conversion reaching 8-bit owners too. Its open island war and dual strategic/action pace made it a landmark Rainbird title and a frequent magazine cover star.

CarVup.history: CarVup is a 1990/1991 vertical platform-racer from Core Design, published for Amiga, Atari ST, and other micros. Instead of a flat track, your cartoon car climbs building-like stages, collecting apples and dodging hazards in a quirky mix of driving and platform timing. Bright graphics and oddball humor fit Core’s early catalog alongside Chuck Rock. On 16-bit machines it was a memorable novelty: short, colorful levels that treated the car more like a mascot platform hero than a simulation vehicle.

Castle Master.history: Castle Master (1990) comes from Incentive Software’s Freescape engine team, known for solid 3D exploration on home computers. Players enter a first-person castle to rescue a sibling, solving puzzles, collecting keys, and fighting spectral guardians across connected 3D rooms. Versions for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, and others showed how Incentive’s filled-polygon tech could support adventure structure as well as earlier shooters like Driller. It gave European micros a distinctive alternative to flat-sprite gothic platformers.

Cauldron.history: Cauldron is a 1985 action-adventure from Palace Software in which a witch flies by broom and explores side-view lands to gather ingredients and confront a pumpkin foe. Mixing shoot-em-up flight sequences with platform exploration, it stood out on Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum, and related machines for its Halloween atmosphere and tough difficulty. Palace’s early hit helped establish the studio before Barbarian. On 8-bit systems it remains a cult favorite of witchy arcade-adventure design.

Cauldron II.history: Cauldron II: The Pumpkin Strikes Back (1986) flips Palace Software’s formula: you control a pumpkin bouncing through a huge castle to defeat the witch. The single continuous map and momentum-based jumping made it more of a precision platform challenge than a broomstick shooter. On Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, Spectrum, and other micros it earned praise for invention and cruelty in equal measure. As a sequel it deepened Palace’s spooky brand and became one of the more unusual British platformers of the mid-1980s.

Champions of Krynn.history: Champions of Krynn (1990) is SSI’s first Dragonlance Gold Box RPG, set in TSR’s Krynn world after the War of the Lance. Party creation, first-person towns and wilderness, and tactical grid combat follow the engine known from Pool of Radiance, with Dragonlance races and orders woven in. Amiga, Commodore 64, and PC versions brought official AD&D Dragonlance play to home computers. It launched a Krynn trilogy and mattered to Amiga/C64 RPG fans who wanted SSI’s deep rules outside the Forgotten Realms.

Championship Manager '93.history: Championship Manager '93 is the early Sports Interactive football-management series entry published by Domark in 1993. Focused on transfers, tactics, and results rather than arcade match graphics, it ran on Amiga and PC and helped define the text-heavy British manager genre. Its growing database feel and addictive season loop built the foundation for later Championship Manager and Football Manager fame. On Amiga it became appointment software for fans who preferred boardroom decisions to on-pitch action games.

Chaos Strikes Back.history: Chaos Strikes Back (1989) is FTL’s expansion-scale follow-up to Dungeon Master, originally for Atari ST and soon on Amiga. It drops a seasoned party into a harsher dungeon of new puzzles, monsters, and item challenges rather than retelling a full beginner campaign. Demanding even by Dungeon Master standards, it rewarded players who had mastered real-time first-person crawling. On ST and Amiga it extended the most influential dungeon-crawler lineage of the late 1980s and kept FTL’s formula at the center of RPG conversations.

Chase H.Q..history: Chase H.Q. is a 1988 Taito arcade driving game in which police pursue criminals, ram their cars to a stop, and clear timed cases. Ocean’s late-80s home conversions brought the siren-blaring chases to Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, and other platforms. Though hardware limits softened arcade polish, the continue-friendly pursuit structure translated well. On European micros it was one of the more recognizable driving licenses of the era, sitting beside Out Run-style racers with a cop-thriller twist.

Chimera.history: Chimera is a 1985 isometric action-adventure published by Firebird, created by Shahid Ahmad. On a doomed spaceship you assemble a bomb while managing oxygen, temperature, and inventory across a compact 3D maze of rooms. Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum, and related versions made it a notable budget-era hit—short to learn, hard to finish. Its Ultimate-like isometric presentation on cheaper tape releases helped spread the style beyond full-price shelves.

Chuck Rock.history: Chuck Rock (1991) is a prehistoric platform beat-em-up from Core Design, published by Virgin on Amiga, Atari ST, and consoles. Belly-bashing caveman Chuck fights through side-scrolling stages of dinosaurs and tribal foes to rescue his partner. Bright cartoon art and slapstick combat made it a mascot-friendly 16-bit showcase for Core. On Amiga it was a high-profile early-90s platformer that helped push the studio toward later Chuck Rock II and other character-led action games.

Chuck Rock II.history: Chuck Rock II: Son of Chuck (1992/1993) continues Core Design’s caveman platform series with Chuck’s offspring as the club-swinging hero. Side-scrolling levels mix combat, simple puzzles, and prehistoric humor across Amiga, Atari ST, and console ports. It refined the cartoon presentation of the first game for the mid-early 1990s 16-bit market. For Amiga owners it extended one of Core’s most visible franchises before the company became better known for Tomb Raider on newer hardware.

Chuckie Egg.history: Chuckie Egg, released in 1983 by A&F Software and designed by Nigel Alderton, is a foundational British platformer. Guide farmer Hen House Harry up ladders and along platforms to collect eggs while avoiding hostile creatures, then face faster variants and a henhouse bonus round. Hits on ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, BBC Micro, and others made it a cross-machine playground staple. Its clean single-screen design influenced countless UK platformers and remained a school-computer legend through the 1980s.

Civilization.history: Sid Meier’s Civilization (1991), from MicroProse, is the landmark turn-based strategy game of guiding a culture from settlement to space race. Expand cities, research technology, negotiate or fight rivals, and balance growth against wonder-building and war. Amiga and other home versions carried the PC phenomenon onto 16-bit machines popular in Europe. On Amiga it became a long-session classic, proving deep 4X strategy could thrive beside action games and helping define the Civilization series’ decades-long influence.

Civilization (AGA).history: Civilization (AGA) refers to the Amiga 1200-era enhanced release of Sid Meier’s Civilization, MicroProse’s 1991 empire-building strategy game. It preserves the turn-based loop of exploration, city management, diplomacy, and tech progress while using AGA hardware for improved color and interface comfort over earlier Amiga builds. For many European players this was the definitive home-computer way to play the original Civ before later PC sequels took over. It kept MicroProse’s flagship strategy experience current on high-end Amigas.

Cobra.history: Cobra is Ocean Software’s 1986 film tie-in based on the Sylvester Stallone action movie. Side-scrolling run-and-gun stages cast players as the vigilante cop clearing streets of gang enemies with guns and knives. Versions for Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum, and other micros were typical of Ocean’s mid-80s license machine: flashy loading screens, tough arcade pacing, and short-lived chart presence. On those platforms it sits among the studio’s many cinema adaptations that dominated UK software charts.

Colonial Conquest.history: Colonial Conquest is a 1985 turn-based strategy game from Strategic Simulations, Inc., simulating great-power rivalry in a late-19th/early-20th-century imperial setting. Players manage armies, navies, and diplomacy across a world map to expand influence. Ports reached Amiga, Atari ST, and other systems after the original computer release, fitting SSI’s wargame and grand-strategy catalog. On 16-bit machines it offered a broader geopolitical sandbox than hex battle scenarios, appealing to strategy fans who wanted empire politics over single-battle tactics.

Colonization.history: Sid Meier’s Colonization (1994), from MicroProse, applies Civilization-style empire building to New World colonization. Found colonies, manage crops and trade, deal with native nations and European rivals, and push toward independence. Amiga versions joined PC as key platforms for the original release generation. On Amiga it was a major mid-90s strategy event—denser economics and politics than many contemporaries—and remains closely associated with Meier’s 1990s MicroProse peak alongside Civilization.

Comic Bakery.history: Comic Bakery is a 1986 Konami action game published in Europe by Imagine Software, especially remembered on the Commodore 64. Guide a baker’s helper through side-view stages, stopping raccoons and keeping production running in a light-hearted industrial setting. Martin Galway’s soundtrack became one of the C64’s celebrated SID scores, often cited as much as the gameplay. Between catchy music and colorful conversion work, it exemplifies mid-80s Konami-to-home computer culture on Commodore machines.

Commando.history: Commando began as Capcom’s 1985 arcade vertical run-and-gun, sending Super Joe up-screen through enemy territory with gunfire and grenades. Elite Systems’ home ports—especially the 1985 Commodore 64 version by Chris Butler—became landmark 8-bit conversions, with Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum, and later Amiga releases following. Rob Hubbard’s C64 music is widely regarded as a SID classic that outgrew the cabinet. On European micros Commando defined the top-down war shooter template for years.

Commando Arcade.history: Commando Arcade is a modern 2014 Commodore 64 homebrew enhancement by the group Nostalgia, built on the classic Elite/Capcom conversion. It expands toward the arcade’s full stage count, retouches graphics and multiplexing, fixes long-standing bugs, and adds new sound options and presentation extras. Rather than a 1980s retail rerelease, it is a contemporary remaster for real C64 hardware and emulators. For fans it became the definitive way to revisit Commando on the machine that made the European home version famous.

Conflict - The Middle East Simulation.history: Conflict: Middle East Political Simulator (often shortened in catalogs) is a 1990 government strategy game by David J. Eastman, published by Virgin Mastertronic for Amiga, Atari ST, and PC. Set in a near-future Middle East crisis, it focuses on diplomacy, intrigue, and policy more than arcade combat—managing a nation’s fate through turn-based decisions. On 16-bit systems it stood out as a serious regional politics sim amid flashier action releases. Strategy players valued its tense what-if framing and dense, text-driven systems.

Continental Circus.history: Continental Circus is a late-1980s Taito Formula One-style arcade racer later converted by Virgin Mastertronic for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, and other homes around 1989. Players race a Grand Prix calendar with qualifying, pit stops, and a continue system tied to finishing position. Home versions aimed to capture the cabinet’s behind-the-car speed within micro limits. On European machines it joined the wave of licensed arcade drivers that filled Christmas charts beside Chase H.Q. and Power Drift.

Crafton & Xunk.history: Crafton & Xunk—exported as Get Dexter—is a 1986 isometric action-adventure by Rémi Herbulot and Michel Rho, published by ERE Informatique. On Amstrad CPC it became a showcase of colorful 3D rooms, object puzzles, and the odd couple of android Crafton and creature Xunk; an Atari ST version followed in 1987. Frequently ranked among the finest CPC adventures, it proved French studios could match Ultimate-style isometrics with sharper style. It remains a landmark of mid-80s Franco-European game design.

Crazy Cars III.history: Crazy Cars III (1992) is a high-speed racing game from French studio Titus, released for Amiga, Atari ST, and PC. Players compete in illegal road races across U.S.-flavored stages, dodging traffic and police while upgrading powerful cars between events. Fast scrolling and flashy 16-bit presentation made it one of Titus’s better-known driving titles. On Amiga it stood as a breakneck early-90s arcade racer, more about thrills and pursuit tension than simulation handling.

Crazy Comets.history: Crazy Comets is a 1985 space shooter published by Martech on the Commodore 64 and other 8-bits, in the vein of Sinistar-style asteroid clearing. Pilot a ship through waves of comets and enemies in brisk arcade action. Its lasting fame on the C64 owes much to Rob Hubbard’s driving soundtrack, a staple of SID anthologies and demo-scene admiration. Gameplay was solid budget-era blasting; the music helped make the title unforgettable on Commodore machines.

Creatures.history: Creatures (1990) is a Commodore 64 platformer from Apex Computer Productions (John and Steve Rowlands), published by Thalamus. Cute fuzzy heroes clash with darkly comic torture-trap set pieces and tough arcade stages—a jarring mix that magazines loved to debate. Strong graphics, animation, and soundtrack made it a late-era C64 showcase. An Amiga conversion appeared later via another team, but the original cemented Apex’s reputation for polished, personality-heavy 8-bit action.

Creatures 2: Torture Trouble.history: Creatures 2: Torture Trouble (1992) is Apex Computer Productions’ Commodore 64 sequel, again published by Thalamus. Fuzzy protagonists must free kin from elaborate torture machines between demanding platform levels, doubling down on the first game’s cute-versus-cruel contrast. Technical sparkle and soundtrack craft kept it among the last great commercial C64 platformers as the market shifted to 16-bit. Planned Amiga work never fully arrived after publisher troubles, leaving the C64 original as the definitive sequel experience.

Creatures II.history: Creatures II is the alternate listing for Apex’s 1992 Commodore 64 sequel better known as Creatures II: Torture Trouble, published by Thalamus. It continues the fuzzy-hero platform formula with interstitial torture-rescue puzzles and highly polished late-era C64 presentation from the Rowlands’ Apex team. As one of the machine’s final big commercial platform hits, it showed 8-bit software could still look and play ambitious in the early 1990s. Home computer fans still cite it beside the first Creatures as Apex’s peak.

Curse of the Azure Bonds.history: Curse of the Azure Bonds (1989) is the second Forgotten Realms Gold Box RPG from SSI, following Pool of Radiance. Characters investigate magical azure bonds forcing them into the schemes of villainous masters, with denser story and iconic AD&D foes. Amiga, Commodore 64, and PC versions spread the campaign widely. On those platforms it deepened SSI’s computer AD&D line and remains a favorite Gold Box entry for its plot hooks and tactical combat.

Cybercon III.history: Cybercon III is a 1991 first-person action-adventure from The Assembly Line, published by US Gold for Amiga, Atari ST, and PC. Inside a vast hostile computer complex you explore free-moving 3D corridors, solve security puzzles, and fight automated defenses to shut down a rogue system. It pushed filled-3D ambition on 16-bit hardware when such engines were still rare in action games. Amiga players remember it as a demanding, atmospheric tech-dungeon from the UK’s experimental early-90s scene.

Cybernoid.history: Cybernoid: The Fighting Machine (1988) is a flip-screen shoot-em-up by Raffaele Cecco, published by Hewson. Pilot a heavily armed ship through fortress corridors packed with guns, bombs, and deadly geometry. Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum, and later 16-bit ports made Cecco’s punishing design famous across British micros. Tight room design and spectacular weapon pickups earned strong reviews; on CPC and Spectrum especially it was a technical showcase of Cecco’s craft.

Cybernoid II.history: Cybernoid II: The Revenge (1988) continues Raffaele Cecco’s Hewson shoot-em-up with new fortress layouts and an expanded arsenal for the fighting machine. Flip-screen exploration and intense defensive firepower again define the challenge on Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum, and other versions. It arrived swiftly after the first game and confirmed Cecco’s style as a Hewson hallmark—beautiful, brutal, and meticulously staged. Micro owners treated the pair as essential late-80s British blasting.

Cybernoid II: The Revenge.history: Cybernoid II: The Revenge, released in 1988 by Hewson and designed by Raffaele Cecco, is the full-titled sequel to Cybernoid. Players again battle through deadly fortress screens with smart bombs, shields, and special weapons against relentless emplacements. Ports across Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64, and 16-bit machines cemented the series’ reputation for ornate difficulty. Among UK shoot-em-ups of the period it stands as a polished second strike rather than a hasty cash-in.

Daley Thompson's Olympic Challenge.history: Daley Thompson's Olympic Challenge (1988) is Ocean’s joystick-waggling sports tie-in built around the decathlete’s Olympic events. Timing and frantic control sequences cover track, field, and discipline minigames branded with Thompson’s fame. Versions for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, and Spectrum followed Ocean’s earlier Daley successes. On those platforms it exemplified late-80s celebrity sports licenses—simple to pick up, exhausting to master, and heavily marketed around a British sporting icon.

Daley Thompson's Supertest.history: Daley Thompson's Supertest (1985) is an earlier Ocean multi-event sports game starring the Olympic decathlon champion. Players tackle a slate of athletic challenges through timing and rapid joystick action on Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum, and related systems. It helped establish Ocean’s Daley Thompson brand before the later Olympic Challenge. As a mid-80s UK chart regular it showed how sports celebrity licenses could drive multi-event compilations on 8-bit computers.

Dark Side.history: Dark Side (1988) is an Incentive Software Freescape title set on a moon base under threat from a weapon platform. First-person 3D exploration, energy management, and puzzle-shooting objectives continue the line begun with Driller and Total Eclipse. Releases for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, and Spectrum spread Incentive’s filled-vector tech widely. On those micros it mattered as proof that home-computer 3D spaces could support paced adventure goals, not only tech demos.

Darkmere.history: Darkmere is a 1994 Amiga action-adventure from Core Design, a late fantasy effort on the platform. Players explore a blighted realm in side-view stages that mix combat, conversation, and item use with a darker tone than Core’s Chuck Rock games. Coming near the end of the Amiga’s commercial prime, it aimed for atmospheric storytelling within action-adventure structure. For Amiga libraries it represents Core’s more serious mid-90s fantasy design before the industry’s attention shifted heavily to PC and consoles.

Das 12. Jahrhundert.history: Das 12. Jahrhundert is a German-language historical strategy game from around 1989–1990 for Atari ST, associated with programmers Theodor Dieckmann and Thomas Lingnau and circulated largely as freeware/public-domain software. Players act as rulers on a stylized map of twelfth-century Europe, managing religion, conquest, and regional power. It reflects the strong German PD and strategy culture on the ST rather than a big boxed Anglo-American release. For Atari ST collectors it is a niche medieval sandbox with period flavor.

Death Knights of Krynn.history: Death Knights of Krynn (1991) is the second game in SSI’s Dragonlance Gold Box trilogy, following Champions of Krynn. Undead armies and Dragonlance lore drive another party-based AD&D adventure with tactical combat and first-person exploration. Amiga, Commodore 64, and PC versions continued Krynn’s computer campaign for home RPG fans. On those platforms it deepened SSI’s early-90s run of official Dungeons & Dragons adaptations before The Dark Queen of Krynn closed the trilogy.

Death Wish 3.history: Death Wish 3 is Gremlin Graphics’ mid-1980s film license based on the Charles Bronson vigilante series, released around 1986–1987 for Amstrad CPC, Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum, and related machines. Openish street-crime action has players cleaning gangs from a decaying city with firearms and improvised weapons. It rode the era’s appetite for violent movie tie-ins while giving Gremlin another chart-oriented license. On 8-bit systems it is remembered as a gritty urban action oddity more than a long-lived franchise starter.

Defender of the Crown.history: Defender of the Crown (1986) is Cinemaware’s landmark medieval strategy-adventure, first famous on the Amiga and then widely ported, including Commodore 64 and Atari ST. Between conquest on an English map, players joust, raid castles, and romance for alliances in a presentation that sold the Amiga’s graphics revolution. It helped define “interactive movie” marketing for 16-bit computers. On Amiga especially it was a pack-in-era showcase that convinced many buyers the machine could deliver cinematic games, not only arcade ports.

Deflektor.history: Deflektor is a reflection puzzle game designed by Costa Panayi and published by Vortex Software in 1987, with later ports to Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and other home machines. Players aim and bounce laser beams off mirrors and gadgets to destroy targets while avoiding deadly feedback. Its clean geometry-driven puzzles stood out beside action-heavy 8-bit catalogues and helped establish Vortex’s reputation for cerebral, tightly designed software on British micros.

Deliverance.history: Deliverance is a 1992 Amiga and Atari ST platform remake by 21st Century Entertainment of Hewson’s 1990 8-bit title Deliverance: Stormlord II. As Stormlord you slash through large levels to free imprisoned fairies and confront returning evil. The 16-bit version rebuilt graphics, sound and pacing for Amiga and ST audiences, keeping the Stormlord fantasy action formula while showcasing what late Hewson/21st Century production could do on those machines.

Delta.history: Delta is a 1987 Commodore 64 horizontal shoot-’em-up by Stavros Fasoulas, published by Thalamus. Piloting a lone fighter through dense alien waves, it was among the polished mid-’80s C64 shmups that matched arcade intensity on home hardware. Rob Hubbard’s soundtrack became one of the system’s best-known game scores and a major reason Delta remains a SID-scene favourite as much as a shooter classic.

Delta Man.history: Delta Man is a late-1980s Commodore 64 post-holocaust action adventure published by Cosmi and designed by Robert Bonifacio. Set in a ruined near-future Chicago, you explore from inside a protective robotic suit, scavenging supplies and dealing with hazards and hostile survivors. Blending first-person exploration screens with joystick-driven commands, it was a distinctive Cosmi survival outing on the C64 rather than a mainstream Amiga or ST hit.

Deluxe Galaga.history: Deluxe Galaga is an Amiga shareware enhancement of Namco’s arcade Galaga by Norwegian developer Edgar M. Vigdal, first released around 1993 and refined through mid-1990s updates. It keeps the formation-shooter core but piles on power-ups, bosses, shops and secrets. Widely regarded as one of the Amiga’s finest freeware titles, it showed how a single author could outshine many commercial ports and remain a fixture of Amiga gaming long after the commercial peak.

Denaris.history: Denaris is Factor 5’s 1988 Amiga R-Type-style horizontal shooter, published by Rainbow Arts. It began life as Katakis; legal pressure over similarity to Irem’s arcade classic led to a rename and adjustments for some markets. With smooth scrolling, strong graphics and Chris Hülsbeck’s music, it became a flagship Amiga shmup and helped cement Factor 5’s early reputation before later console work.

Die Siedler.history: Die Siedler (The Settlers) is Blue Byte’s 1993 Amiga real-time strategy and city-building game designed by Volker Wertich. Players expand a medieval settlement by chaining goods production through an intricate economy of serfs and workshops. Its charming isometric world and logistics-focused play made it a landmark German Amiga strategy title and the start of a long-running series that defined cozy empire building for many European players.

Disposable Hero.history: Disposable Hero is a 1993 Amiga shoot-’em-up developed by Euphoria and published by Gremlin Graphics. A heavily armed craft battles through horizontally scrolling stages packed with enemy craft and large bosses. Aimed at late Amiga hardware and showmanship, it arrived as the platform’s commercial shooters were peaking and remains a showcase of Gremlin-era Amiga arcade conversion ambition.

Dive Bomber.history: Dive Bomber (also known in some markets as Spitfire) is a late-1980s World War II flight combat game from Accolade/Firebird circles, appearing on Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST and PC. Missions mix cockpit flying, bombing runs and carrier operations in a semi-simulation presentation. It brought accessible wartime aerial action to 8- and 16-bit homes when flight games were a major selling genre on those platforms.

Dizzy: The Ultimate Cartoon Adventure.history: Dizzy: The Ultimate Cartoon Adventure launched the Dizzy series in 1987 from the Oliver Twins and Codemasters. The egg-shaped hero explores cartoon fantasy screens collecting items and solving inventory puzzles. Born on the ZX Spectrum and widely ported to C64, Amstrad CPC and later machines, it helped define budget adventure-platform hybrids and spawned one of Britain’s most recognisable 8-bit mascot franchises.

Dominator.history: Dominator is a 1989 shoot-’em-up from System 3, released on Commodore 64, Amiga and Atari ST. It mixes horizontally scrolling blasting with tougher set-piece sections and a slick late-’80s presentation. As System 3 pushed arcade polish onto home computers, Dominator joined the wave of ambitious European shmups competing for magazine cover attention on 8- and 16-bit systems.

Donkey Kong Junior.history: Donkey Kong Junior is Nintendo’s 1982 arcade sequel to Donkey Kong, later ported to home computers and consoles including Commodore platforms in various forms. You climb vines and platforms as Junior to rescue Donkey Kong from Mario. Alongside the original, it helped bring Nintendo’s platform template to living rooms and remains a key early arcade-to-home conversion in many retro libraries.

Doomdark's Revenge.history: Doomdark’s Revenge is Mike Singleton’s 1984 sequel to The Lords of Midnight, published by Beyond for ZX Spectrum and Commodore 64. An epic strategy-adventure across a vast map of tribes and landscapes, it expanded the landmark landscape-engine warfare of its predecessor. On British 8-bit machines it stood as one of the most ambitious fantasy campaigns of the mid-1980s.

Double Dragon.history: Double Dragon began as Technōs Japan’s 1987 arcade beat-’em-up and reached Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and many other homes through licensed ports. Two martial artists fight through urban stages to rescue a kidnapped ally, popularising cooperative side-scrolling brawling. Home versions varied in fidelity, but the name became shorthand for the genre across late-’80s computer gaming.

Draconus.history: Draconus is a 1988 arcade adventure from Zeppelin Games for Commodore 64 and ZX Spectrum. Exploring a labyrinth of caverns and castles as a mythical creature, players fight, collect items and uncover routes in a flick-screen style common to British budget houses. It exemplified Zeppelin’s value-priced C64 and Spectrum action adventures of the late 1980s.

Dragon Breed.history: Dragon Breed is Irem’s 1989 arcade horizontal shooter, later converted to Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and other micros by Activision and partners. You ride a dragon that doubles as both mount and extendable weapon through fantasy stages. Home ports brought Irem’s ornate arcade design to European 16-bit and 8-bit owners hungry for coin-op shooters beyond sci-fi settings.

Dragon Ninja.history: Dragon Ninja is the European home-computer branding of Data East’s Bad Dudes Vs. DragonNinja arcade beat-’em-up, widely released by Imagine/Ocean on Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and Amstrad CPC around 1988–89. Ninjas battle street enemies and bosses to rescue a kidnapped president. Ocean’s aggressive arcade conversion program made it a familiar high-street title across UK 8- and 16-bit machines.

Dragon Wars.history: Dragon Wars is a party-based fantasy role-playing game from Interplay, released around 1989–90 on Commodore 64, Amiga, PC and other platforms. Designed in the spirit of the Bard’s Tale lineage, it offers dense city and dungeon exploration with tactical combat. On the C64 and Amiga it was a late flowering of classic Western CRPG design as the genre migrated toward 16-bit machines.

Dragonflight.history: Dragonflight is a 1990 role-playing game from German developer Thalion Software for Amiga and Atari ST. It combines overhead and exploratory RPG elements with a dragon-riding fantasy theme and the polished presentation typical of Thalion’s early catalogue. For ST and Amiga owners in continental Europe it was part of the wave of ambitious local RPGs competing with British and American imports.

DreamWeb.history: DreamWeb is a 1994 cyberpunk point-and-click adventure by Creative Reality, published by Empire Interactive for Amiga and PC. Set in a grim near-future city, it mixes investigation, inventory puzzles and a mature tone uncommon in many Amiga adventures. Late in the Amiga’s commercial life it stood out as a dark, adult-oriented graphic adventure for players seeking something beyond lighter fantasy fare.

Driller.history: Driller is Incentive Software’s 1987 3D exploration game built with the Freescape engine, released on ZX Spectrum, Amstrad CPC, Commodore 64, Amiga and Atari ST. Players navigate solid-filled 3D landscapes placing drilling rigs to avert planetary disaster. It was a pioneering showcase of filled-vector worlds on 8-bit micros and helped launch Freescape as a technical landmark of late-’80s British software.

Dune.history: Dune is Cryo Interactive’s 1992 adventure and strategy hybrid based on Frank Herbert’s novel, released on Amiga and PC among other platforms. Players take the role of Paul Atreides, mixing dialogue, exploration and spice-management strategy on Arrakis. Its cinematic presentation and licensed lore made it a distinctive Amiga narrative experience alongside more action-driven genre titles of the early 1990s.

Dune II.history: Dune II: The Building of a Dynasty (1992) from Westwood Studios is widely credited with defining the modern real-time strategy template: base building, resource harvesting and faction warfare on Arrakis. The original PC hit reshaped strategy gaming; Amiga owners later received a tailored version under the Battle for Arrakis name. Its influence on Command & Conquer and the RTS boom makes it one of the decade’s pivotal strategy designs.

Dune II: The Battle for Arrakis.history: Dune II: The Battle for Arrakis is the 1993 Amiga edition of Westwood’s landmark real-time strategy game Dune II. Adapted for Amiga hardware and European packaging, it brought base-building spice wars between House Atreides, Harkonnen and Ordos to a huge Amiga audience. For many Amiga players it was the definitive way to experience the title that set the blueprint for 1990s RTS games.

Dungeon Master.history: Dungeon Master, released by FTL Games in 1987 first on Atari ST and soon after on Amiga, reinvented the computer dungeon crawl with real-time first-person party combat and immersive sound. Exploring a multi-level labyrinth, players manage inventory, spells and hungry adventurers under constant threat. It became a defining ST and Amiga RPG and inspired countless real-time dungeon clones through the early 1990s.

Dungeon Master Expansion Set I - Chaos S.history: Chaos Strikes Back (1989) is FTL’s expansion-scale follow-up to Dungeon Master for Atari ST and Amiga. Importing heroes from a completed campaign, it drops them into a far harsher dungeon of puzzles and combat. For ST and Amiga owners who had mastered the original, it extended the landmark real-time crawler with notorious difficulty and cemented the series’ cult status.

Dyna Blaster.history: Dyna Blaster is the European name for Hudson Soft’s Bomberman, with a celebrated early-1990s Amiga multiplayer conversion (often linked with Ubisoft publishing). Up to several players plant bombs in maze arenas to blast walls and rivals. Hot-seat and multi-joystick sessions made it a party staple on Amiga, turning a Japanese arcade/console concept into one of the platform’s essential social games.

Dynablaster.history: Dynablaster is another common European spelling of Dyna Blaster, the Amiga-era Bomberman multiplayer hit derived from Hudson Soft’s series. Friends race through brick mazes laying bombs, grabbing power-ups and cornering opponents. On Amiga it was prized less as a single-player campaign than as a living-room versus classic that kept machines switched on long after solo adventures ended.

Elevator Action.history: Elevator Action is Taito’s 1983 arcade spy-action game, later ported to home computers including Commodore systems and other micros. Agent Otto sneaks through a building via elevators and escalators, collecting documents and shooting enemy agents. Compact, readable stages made it a frequent early arcade conversion on 8-bit platforms and a recognisable Taito classic in retro collections.

Elfmania.history: Elfmania is a 1994 Amiga one-on-one fighter by Finnish studio Terramarque, published by Renegade Software. Beyond versus bouts it layers an unusual economy: win coins, hire stronger elves and contest a map toward the throne. Colourful Amiga presentation and odd strategic structure made it a cult curiosity; Terramarque later merged into what became Housemarque.

Eliminator.history: Eliminator is a 1988 tube-style 3D shoot-’em-up from Hewson Consultants for Amiga, Atari ST and Commodore 64. Racing along a ribbon of track, players blast obstacles and enemies in a high-speed corridor presentation. It showcased Hewson’s knack for flashy technical demos that still played as arcade games on late-’80s 16-bit and C64 hardware.

Elite.history: Elite, created by David Braben and Ian Bell and first released by Acornsoft in 1984, is the seminal open-ended space trading and combat simulator. Wireframe 3D ships, reputation and a galaxy of markets defined a new kind of freedom on home computers. Ports to Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST and many others spread its influence; it remains a foundational title for sandbox space games.

Elvira - Mistress of the Dark.history: Elvira: Mistress of the Dark is a 1990 horror adventure from Horror Soft (later Adventure Soft), published with Accolade on Amiga, Atari ST, PC and Commodore 64. Mixing inventory puzzles with combat inside a cursed castle tied to the Elvira horror hostess licence, it pushed gory presentation on 16-bit machines and helped establish Horror Soft’s dark adventure brand before later Waxworks-era titles.

Emlyn Hughes International Soccer.history: Emlyn Hughes International Soccer is Audiogenic’s football game, launched on Commodore 64 in 1988 and later converted to Amiga and other formats. Endorsed by the former England captain, it emphasised fluid side-on play and became a C64 football favourite in the UK. On Amiga it continued Audiogenic’s push to bring its 8-bit sports success onto 16-bit hardware.

Enchanted Land.history: Enchanted Land is a 1990 fantasy platformer from Thalion Software for Amiga and Atari ST. Players explore colourful stages battling creatures and collecting magic in a polished Teutonic 16-bit style. It sits among Thalion’s early catalogue that gave German Amiga and ST owners home-grown arcade adventures with strong audiovisual presentation.

Enduro Racer.history: Enduro Racer is Sega’s 1986 off-road motorcycle arcade racer, converted to ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and other homes by Activision and partners. Riders jump hills and weave through traffic in pseudo-3D courses. Home ports brought a slice of Sega’s mid-’80s arcade racing to European micros when coin-op licences dominated Christmas charts.

Enforcer.history: Enforcer: Fullmetal Megablaster is a 1992 Commodore 64 horizontal shoot-’em-up by Manfred Trenz (as “The Master”), released on CP Verlag’s Golden Disk magazine. A spiritual follow-up to Katakis with weapon upgrades and large bosses, it was Trenz’s late C64 showcase after Turrican fame. For many 64 owners it remains a high-water mark of early-’90s German magazine software.

Enforcer: Fullmetal Megablaster.history: Enforcer: Fullmetal Megablaster (1992) is Manfred Trenz’s Commodore 64 horizontal shmup published via CP Verlag’s Golden Disk line, with music by Markus Siebold. Often treated as an unofficial Katakis successor, it delivers polished scrolling combat and power-ups on ageing 8-bit hardware. It stands as a late commercial-quality C64 shooter from the creator of Turrican and Katakis.

Enigma Force.history: Enigma Force is Beyond’s 1985 sequel to Shadowfire for Commodore 64 and ZX Spectrum. Controlling a squad through icon-driven adventure and combat after the events of the first game, it continued Beyond’s experiments with accessible tactical storytelling on 8-bit machines. Together with Shadowfire it remains a notable mid-’80s British hybrid of adventure interface and squad action.

Epic.history: Epic is a 1992 space combat game from Digital Image Design, published by Ocean for Amiga and PC. Large-scale missions, cinematic cutscenes and polygonal ships aimed to deliver a Hollywood space-war spectacle on home computers. Despite mixed reaction to difficulty and structure, its Amiga presentation made it a memorable Ocean-era showcase of early-’90s 16-bit ambition.

Equinox.history: Equinox is a 1986 action-puzzle game published by Mikro-Gen for ZX Spectrum, Amstrad CPC and Commodore 64, programmed by Raffaele Cecco and Chris Hinsley. Guiding a disposal droid through contaminated facilities, players shut down security and clear radioactive waste under time pressure. It highlighted Cecco’s early craft on British 8-bit platforms before later Hewson hits.

European Football Champ.history: European Football Champ is a early-1990s football title tied to Taito’s arcade soccer lineage and home conversions aimed at European computer audiences, including Amiga and other micros. Side-scrolling match play and big sprites chased the coin-op feel of contemporary arcade football. It joined a crowded field of licensed and arcade-style soccer games competing for joystick time on Amiga and 8-bit systems.

Exile.history: Exile is a landmark action-adventure by Peter Irvin and Jeremy Smith, released in 1988 on BBC Micro and Acorn Electron and later on Commodore 64, Amiga and Atari ST. Its cavernous world uses convincing physics for jetpacking, objects and combat. On Amiga and C64 it became a cult classic for deep, systemic exploration rarely matched by simpler platform adventures.

Exolon.history: Exolon is Raffaele Cecco’s 1987 run-and-gun platformer published by Hewson for ZX Spectrum, Amstrad CPC and Commodore 64, with later 16-bit appearances. A heavily armed trooper fights across alien landscapes collecting suits and weapons. Its chunky Spectrum graphics and tough arcade pacing made it one of Hewson’s signature 8-bit action games of the late 1980s.

Eye of the Beholder.history: Eye of the Beholder (1990–91) is a Dungeons & Dragons real-time dungeon crawler developed by Westwood Studios and published by Strategic Simulations. First-person party exploration under AD&D rules brought Gold Box-era D&D to a Dungeon Master-like presentation on PC, Amiga and other platforms. It became one of the most popular licensed RPGs on Amiga and helped popularise real-time AD&D crawling.

Eye of the Beholder II.history: Eye of the Beholder II: The Legend of Darkmoon (1991) continues Westwood and SSI’s real-time AD&D dungeon series on PC, Amiga and related platforms. Players delve into a temple stronghold with improved presentation and tougher Adventurers’ Guild-style progression. On Amiga it extended one of the platform’s most played licensed RPG lines into a fuller sequel campaign.

Eye of the Beholder II: The Legend of Da.history: Eye of the Beholder II: The Legend of Darkmoon is the 1991 sequel to Westwood Studios’ SSI-published Dungeons & Dragons crawler. Real-time first-person combat and exploration return in a larger temple complex tied to Forgotten Realms lore. Amiga and PC releases made it a centrepiece AD&D experience for 16-bit RPG fans who had finished the original Beholder.

F-19 Stealth Fighter.history: F-19 Stealth Fighter is MicroProse’s late-1980s combat flight simulation of a fictional stealth aircraft, released on PC, Commodore 64, Amiga and Atari ST. Missions emphasise radar avoidance, weapons management and Cold War theatres. Typical of MicroProse’s simulation depth, it brought serious jet-combat play to Amiga and ST owners alongside Sid Meier–era strategy hits from the same publisher.

F-29 Retaliator.history: F-29 Retaliator is a 1990 combat flight game from Digital Image Design, published by Ocean for Amiga, Atari ST and PC. Featuring futuristic and near-future fighters, it offered fast polygon combat and flashy presentation aimed at action-oriented sim fans. On Amiga it was a high-profile Ocean flight title in the same era as DID’s other technical showpieces.

Fairlight.history: Fairlight is a 1985 isometric action-adventure by Bo Jangeborg, published by The Edge for ZX Spectrum and later ported to Amstrad CPC, Commodore 64 and other formats. Exploring castle halls with object physics and combat, it was celebrated for its Spectrum graphics tech. It became a touchstone of mid-’80s British isometric adventures on 8-bit machines.

Fantasy World Dizzy.history: Fantasy World Dizzy (1989) is a Codemasters adventure-platform entry in the Oliver Twins’ Dizzy series, widely released on Spectrum, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, Amiga and Atari ST. Dizzy explores a fairy-tale kingdom solving item puzzles across cartoon screens. Often cited as a high point of the series, it helped cement Dizzy as a budget-era British mascot across 8- and 16-bit formats.

Feud.history: Feud is a 1987 action-strategy game by Binary Design, published by Mastertronic on ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and other platforms. Two rival wizards roam a village gathering herbs to brew spells and outwit each other. As an affordable Mastertronic title it brought compact magical rivalry to budget shelves and remains a cult favourite of late-’80s 8-bit gaming.

Fightin' Spirit.history: Fightin’ Spirit is a 1996 Amiga one-on-one fighting game by Italian developer Light Shock Software, published by neo Software for OCS/ECS, AGA and CD32. With a roster of special-move fighters and Neo Geo-inspired polish, it arrived late but is often named among the Amiga’s best versus fighters. It showed the platform could still host credible Street Fighter-style games near the end of its commercial run.

Fire & Ice.history: Fire & Ice is a 1992 Amiga platformer by Graftgold, published by Renegade, with later conversions including Atari ST.
