On European 16-bit machines it was a solid arcade flyer amid the R-Type generation of ports.

Pac-Mania.history: Pac-Mania (1987) is Namco’s isometric arcade reinvention of Pac-Man, adding jumping and pseudo-3D mazes. Grandslam and other publishers converted it for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, and Spectrum, giving home players a fresh take on the maze icon. Among late-1980s Namco ports it stood out for visual novelty and helped keep Pac-Man relevant on 8- and 16-bit computers.

Pacman on E's.history: Pacman on E’s is a late Atari STE shareware Pac-Man clone by Stuart Innes, written in 68000 assembler to exploit the STE’s blitter, DMA sound, and extended palette. It offers large level sets, sampled audio, and two-player options in a neon rave-styled package rather than a licensed Namco port. Clearly a scene/homebrew-era STE title, it shows how Atari enthusiasts kept arcade maze games alive with machine-specific flair.

Pang.history: Pang (also known as Buster Bros. or Pomping World) is Mitchell’s late-1980s arcade hit about bursting balloons with a harpoon across single-screen stages. Ocean’s early-1990s conversions for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, and consoles became hugely popular in Europe for co-op play. On home computers it was one of the most addictive two-player arcade ports of its generation.

Panza Kick Boxing.history: Panza Kick Boxing (1990), from Futura and Loriciel and tied to trainer Roger Panza, is a digitized martial-arts fighter for Amiga, Atari ST, and PC. It emphasises realistic kickboxing timing and training options over fantasy special moves. Alongside related European fighters of the period, it gave 16-bit owners a more “sports sim” take on one-on-one combat before morphing into Best of the Best in some markets.

Paperboy.history: Atari Games’ Paperboy (1984) cast players as a bike courier delivering papers while dodging suburbia’s hazards in an isometric view. Elite Systems and others ported it widely to Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST, Amstrad CPC, and Spectrum. The quirky premise and high-score chase made it one of the more distinctive arcade conversions on 8-bit and 16-bit home machines through the late 1980s.

Paradroid.history: Paradroid (1985), designed by Andrew Braybrook for Graftgold and Hewson, is a Commodore 64 classic about clearing a spaceship of hostile robots. Influence devices let you seize stronger droids, while the famous transfer game decides control in a tense logic duel. Its depth, atmosphere, and technical polish made it a defining C64 action-strategy hybrid and a cornerstone of Braybrook’s reputation.

Paradroid 90.history: Paradroid 90 (1990) updates Andrew Braybrook’s Paradroid for Amiga and Atari ST with sharper graphics, smoother control, and the same robot-possession fantasy aboard a hostile freighter. Graftgold and Hewson brought the C64 cult hit to 16-bit hardware without losing the transfer-game tension. It became the definitive way many ST and Amiga owners experienced one of Britain’s great 8-bit designs.

Parallax.history: Parallax (1986), from Sensible Software and published by Ocean, is a multidirectional shoot-’em-up and exploration game for the Commodore 64 (with other versions). Piloting a craft across alien landscapes, players mix shooting with on-foot terminal hacking. Early Sensible inventiveness and a strong soundtrack made it a notable C64 original before the team’s later sports and sim fame.

Perihelion.history: Perihelion (1993), published by Psygnosis, is a dark science-fantasy RPG for the Amiga blending first-person dungeon travel, psychic combat, and bleak narrative tone. Its elaborate magic system and gothic presentation aimed at players wanting atmosphere beyond high-fantasy clones. As a late OCS/ECS-era Psygnosis RPG it remains a cult Amiga title for mood and ambition more than mass-market success.

Phantasie III - The Wrath of Nikademus.history: Phantasie III: The Wrath of Nikademus (1987), from Strategic Simulations (SSI), concludes the early Phantasie CRPG trilogy with party adventuring, tactical fights, and a final confrontation against the dark lord Nikademus. Ports reached Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, and other systems popular with European RPG fans. It helped establish SSI’s pre–Gold Box fantasy line on home computers hungry for multi-character campaigns.

Phantoms of the Asteroid.history: Phantoms of the Asteroid (1985–86), published by Mastertronic, is a budget space adventure-shooter for Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum, and Amstrad CPC. Explore asteroid interiors, manage resources, and survive hostile encounters in a compact sci-fi package sold at pocket-money prices. On the C64, Rob Hubbard’s music again lifted a Mastertronic title into lasting memory beyond its simple mechanics.

Pinball Dreams.history: Pinball Dreams (1992), from Digital Illusions and 21st Century Entertainment, proved that software pinball could feel serious on the Amiga with multiple tables, multiball, and thumping sound. It helped launch the studio that later became DICE and sparked a wave of Amiga pinball clones and sequels. For many players it is the moment home-computer pinball stopped being a novelty and became a genre.

Pinball Fantasies.history: Pinball Fantasies (1992), the follow-up from Digital Illusions and 21st Century, refined Amiga pinball with new tables, sharper physics, and bigger production values soon after Pinball Dreams. It cemented the series as the gold standard for 16-bit digital pinball in Europe. Sequels and enhanced editions kept the brand alive through AGA and CD32 hardware upgrades.

Pinball Fantasies (AGA).history: Pinball Fantasies’ AGA edition updates the 1992 Digital Illusions classic for Amiga 1200/4000 chipsets with richer colours and smoother presentation while keeping the same celebrated tables. It let next-generation Amiga owners enjoy the definitive early-1990s pinball package without abandoning the original design. In retro libraries the AGA label marks the enhanced 32-bit-era release of an already landmark title.

Pinball Fantasies (CD32).history: The CD32 version of Pinball Fantasies brings Digital Illusions’ Amiga pinball hit to Commodore’s console with CD delivery and machine-specific packaging of the familiar tables. It was part of the early-1990s push to stock the CD32 with proven Amiga crowd-pleasers. For console Amiga households it offered the series’ slick multiball action without floppy swapping.

Pinball Illusions.history: Pinball Illusions (1995), again from Digital Illusions and 21st Century, pushed Amiga pinball into the AGA and CD32 era with denser graphics, multiball spectacle, and new table themes. It arrived as a late flagship for the platform’s pinball boom when many developers were already leaving for PC and consoles. Alongside Dreams and Fantasies it completes the trilogy most associated with Amiga digital pinball.

Pirates!.history: Sid Meier’s Pirates! (1987), published by MicroProse, blends fencing, sailing, trading, and gubernatorial politics into an open-ended Caribbean sandbox. The Commodore 64 original and later Amiga and ST versions turned swashbuckling into a personal career rather than a single mission. It became one of MicroProse’s most beloved non-combat sims and a model for sandbox adventure on 8- and 16-bit computers.

Pit-Fighter.history: Pit-Fighter (1990) was Atari Games’ digitized-sprites arcade brawler, and Domark brought home versions to Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, and other formats. Fighters clash in illegal pit matches using captured footage aesthetics that looked startling beside hand-drawn sprites. On European micros it joined the early-1990s wave of “photo-real” sports and fight conversions, even when animation fidelity varied by platform.

Platoon.history: Platoon (1987–88), Ocean Software’s multi-load adaptation of Oliver Stone’s Vietnam film, appeared on Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST, Amstrad CPC, and Spectrum. Distinct sections cover jungle patrols, village tension, and bunker assaults rather than a single gameplay mode. It became one of Ocean’s defining serious film licences on 8-bit machines, remembered for atmosphere and for Robert T. Clark’s C64 soundtrack as much as for its difficulty.

Pool of Radiance.history: Pool of Radiance (1988), from Strategic Simulations, launched the Gold Box line of official Advanced Dungeons & Dragons CRPGs, set in the Forgotten Realms city of Phlan. Party creation, first-person exploration, and tactical AD&D combat reached Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST, and PC owners in force. It mattered as the breakthrough that made tabletop D&D feel authentic on late-1980s home computers and spawned a long series of sequels.

Populous.history: Populous is Bullfrog Productions’ landmark 1989 god game, designed by Peter Molyneux and published by Electronic Arts on Amiga, Atari ST and other platforms. Players raise and lower land, guide tribes and unleash disasters as a deity competing for worshippers. Its isometric living world and indirect control defined a new strategy subgenre and made the Amiga a showcase for ambitious British simulation design.

Populous II.history: Populous II is Bullfrog’s 1991 sequel to the original god game, released on Amiga, Atari ST and PC with Electronic Arts. Set among Greek-inspired deities, it expands divine powers, effects and multiplayer rivalry while keeping the raise-and-sculpt landscape core. On 16-bit machines it refined one of the Amiga’s defining strategy franchises and cemented Bullfrog’s early-’90s reputation.

Populous II: Trials of the Olympian Gods.history: Populous II: Trials of the Olympian Gods is the full title of Bullfrog’s 1991 sequel, published by Electronic Arts for Amiga, Atari ST and PC. As an Olympian deity you reshape terrain, cast devastating spells and grow a following against rival gods. Richer effects and scenario structure made it a high-water mark for Amiga god games and a natural follow-up to the series’ breakthrough.

Power Drift.history: Power Drift is Sega’s 1988 arcade racing game, later converted for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and other homes by Activision and partners. Drivers race wild multi-car tracks with banked turns and airborne jumps in a cartoonish superscaler style. The home ports brought a flashy coin-op racer to European micros when arcade conversions were a major Amiga and ST selling point.

Power Tetris.history: Power Tetris is a late-1980s/early-1990s home-computer variant of Alexey Pajitnov’s Tetris formula, appearing in European catalogues on platforms such as the Amiga and related micros. It keeps falling-block stacking and line clears while adding power-oriented presentation or rule twists typical of unofficial clones of the era. Like many regional Tetris editions, it shows how the puzzle craze spread across Amiga and 8-bit libraries beyond the official Spectrum Holobyte/Mirrorsoft line.

Powermonger.history: Powermonger is Bullfrog’s 1990 real-time strategy game, designed by Peter Molyneux’s team and published by Electronic Arts on Amiga, Atari ST and PC. Commanding a conquering force across linked landscapes, you manage armies, resources and diplomacy in a living 3D-looking world. Coming after Populous, it pushed Amiga strategy toward denser simulation and helped define Bullfrog’s early EA-era catalogue.

PowerMonger.history: PowerMonger (stylised PowerMonger) is Bullfrog Productions’ 1990 conquest strategy title for Amiga, Atari ST and PC, published by Electronic Arts. Players expand influence by capturing settlements, assigning work and fighting rival leaders in a continuous campaign map. It stood beside Populous as a flagship Amiga god-strategy outing and showcased Bullfrog’s knack for systemic, spectacle-driven war games.

Prehistorik.history: Prehistorik is Titus Interactive’s 1991 platformer, released on Amiga, Atari ST, Amstrad CPC, Commodore 64 and PC. A cartoon caveman clubs dinosaurs, gathers food and explores prehistoric levels with light puzzle touches. Bright graphics and slapstick humour made it a popular early-’90s European platformer, especially on CPC and Amiga shelves dominated by French publishers.

Prehistorik 2.history: Prehistorik 2 is Titus’s 1993 sequel to the caveman platformer, arriving on Amiga, Atari ST, PC and other systems. Larger levels, improved animation and more collectible-driven play expanded the cartoon prehistoric formula. It was a late commercial Amiga/ST platform hit from Titus and kept the series visible as 16-bit homes competed with consoles.

Prehistorik II.history: Prehistorik II is the Roman-numeral styling of Titus Interactive’s 1993 Prehistorik sequel for Amiga, Atari ST, PC and related platforms. You guide a stone-age hero through colourful stages, smashing foes and stockpiling food. As a polished French platform sequel it reinforced Titus’s presence on European Amiga and CPC-era catalogues into the mid-1990s.

Prince of Persia.history: Prince of Persia is Jordan Mechner’s 1989 cinematic platformer, originally for Apple II and widely ported to Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, CPC and more by Broderbund and partners. Rotoscoped animation, deadly traps and a ticking escape narrative set a new standard for fluid character movement. On Amiga and ST it became a defining showcase of storytelling platform design and one of the era’s most influential adventure-action games.

Project Firestart.history: Project Firestart is a 1989 Commodore 64 science-fiction horror adventure developed by Dynamix and published by Electronic Arts. Aboard a derelict research ship you explore corridors, gather logs and confront a genetic nightmare with limited combat and multiple endings. Rare for the C64, it blended cinematic pacing with survival tension and remains a cult highlight of late 8-bit narrative design.

Project Stealth Fighter.history: Project Stealth Fighter is MicroProse’s mid-1980s combat flight simulation for the Commodore 64 (and related 8-bit machines), designed in the Sid Meier/Arnold era of the company’s catalogue. Piloting a fictional stealth fighter, players fly Cold War–style missions with radar evasion and air-to-ground strikes. It helped prove serious jet sims could work on the C64 and directly led toward the later F-19 Stealth Fighter line.

Project-X.history: Project-X is Team17’s 1992 Amiga horizontal shoot-’em-up, also seen on Atari ST and later platforms. A heavily armed fighter battles dense waves, power-ups and huge bosses across polished sci-fi stages. Known for toughness and presentation, it became one of the Amiga’s flagship shmups and a signature early Team17 arcade title before the studio’s Worms fame.

Purple Saturn Day.history: Purple Saturn Day is a 1989 psychedelic sports anthology by Exxos (ERE Informatique / Infogrames circles), released on Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and other systems. Alien contests mix racing, reflex challenges and surreal arena events under a distinctive French art-and-music aesthetic. It stood out on European 16-bit machines as experimental multimedia sport rather than a conventional licensed athletics game.

Pushover.history: Pushover is a 1992 puzzle game by Red Rat and Ocean Software for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and PC, starring an ant rearranging domino-like blocks. Each screen is a timing-and-path puzzle: tip the right sequence so the cascade reaches the exit. Clever level design and charming presentation made it a favourite Amiga/ST brain-teaser amid the early-’90s puzzle boom.

Puzzle Bobble.history: Puzzle Bobble (known as Bust-A-Move in some regions) is Taito’s 1994 arcade puzzle game spun from Bubble Bobble, later ported to home computers and consoles including Amiga. Players aim coloured bubbles to match and clear clusters before they reach the bottom. Its simple aiming skill and escalating boards made it a defining mid-’90s puzzle hit and a late Amiga arcade conversion favourite.

Quiz Master.history: Quiz Master is a general-knowledge quiz title that appeared in various 8- and 16-bit home-computer catalogues, typically presenting multiple-choice or typed answers across subject rounds. On Amiga, ST and British micros, such quiz packages filled a popular niche for party and family software beside action games. It reflects the era’s appetite for trivia entertainment on machines that doubled as living-room computers.

R-Type.history: R-Type is Irem’s landmark 1987 arcade horizontal shoot-’em-up, famously converted to Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST, Amstrad CPC and other homes. Piloting the R-9 fighter, players master the Force pod, charge shots and meticulously patterned bosses. Home ports—especially Electric Dreams/Activision-era versions—were prestige Amiga and ST showpieces and helped define the European shmup gold standard.

R-Type II.history: R-Type II is Irem’s 1989 arcade sequel, later brought to Amiga and Atari ST by Arc Developments and Activision. It expands weapons, stages and boss spectacles while keeping the Force-device tactical core of the original. On 16-bit computers it was a sought-after conversion that proved Amiga and ST audiences still demanded arcade-faithful shooters into the early 1990s.

Raid on Bungeling Bay.history: Raid on Bungeling Bay is Will Wright’s 1984 action game, published by Brøderbund on Commodore 64 and later other platforms. Flying a helicopter, you bomb factories across an island war zone while managing fuel and enemy defences. Its living map and systemic destruction foreshadowed Wright’s SimCity work and made it a notable early C64 design landmark beyond simple shooters.

Railroad Tycoon.history: Railroad Tycoon is Sid Meier’s 1990 business strategy classic from MicroProse, released on PC, Amiga, Atari ST and other systems. Players build track networks, manage trains and compete for industrial dominance across historical maps. On Amiga and ST it brought deep economic simulation to 16-bit strategy fans and helped establish the tycoon genre that followed.

Rainbow Islands.history: Rainbow Islands is Taito’s 1987 arcade sequel to Bubble Bobble, widely ported to Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, CPC and more. Bub and Bob, restored to human form, climb vertical islands by firing rainbows that double as weapons and platforms. Charming conversion quality—especially on Amiga—made it a beloved European home hit and a high point of cute’em-up platforming.

Rambo III.history: Rambo III is Ocean Software’s late-1980s movie licence game tied to the Sylvester Stallone film, released on Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, CPC and other formats. Missions mix infiltration, combat and vehicle sections reflecting the Afghanistan-set story. Typical of Ocean’s big film adaptations, it was a high-profile Amiga and 8-bit shelf title driven by cinema branding as much as gameplay.

Rambo: First Blood Part II.history: Rambo: First Blood Part II is Ocean’s mid-1980s licensed action game based on the second Rambo film, appearing on Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and related micros. Stages typically cover jungle infiltration, combat and rescue themes from the movie. It was part of Ocean’s early wave of British film tie-ins that dominated 8-bit charts and magazine covers.

Rasputin.history: Rasputin is a 1986 isometric puzzle-adventure published by Firebird for ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Amstrad CPC. Players navigate a mystical fortress of rooms, collecting jewels and confronting guardians linked to the infamous mystic’s legend. Its detailed 3D-style rooms and tricky progression marked it as an ambitious budget-era British adventure on the major 8-bit machines.

Red Storm Rising.history: Red Storm Rising is MicroProse’s late-1980s submarine warfare simulation based on Tom Clancy’s novel, designed with Sid Meier’s involvement for Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST and PC. Commanding a modern attack sub, you hunt Soviet shipping across North Atlantic scenarios with sensors, torpedoes and careful tactics. It was a flagship C64/Amiga military sim and a high point of licensed Clancy strategy on home computers.

Renegade.history: Renegade is the Western home version of Technos’ arcade beat-’em-up Nekketsu Kōha Kunio-kun, converted by Imagine/Ocean for Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum, Amiga and Atari ST. Street brawling across stages of thugs established the side-view fighter template for many European players. On 8-bit machines especially, it was a foundational belt-scrolling combat hit of the late 1980s.

Reunion.history: Reunion is a 1994 Amiga (and PC) science-fiction strategy game by Amnesty Design / Grandslam, blending empire building, research and tactical combat. After humanity’s colonies are lost, you rebuild civilisation across planets and manage diplomacy and war. Ambitious scope and late-Amiga production values made it a notable European space-strategy outing as the platform’s commercial era wound down.

Rick Dangerous.history: Rick Dangerous is Core Design’s 1989 platformer, published by Firebird/Rainbird for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, CPC and other systems. Inspired by pulp serials and Indiana Jones, it packs trap-filled temples, precise jumps and cheeky humour. Brutal but memorable level design made it a cult Amiga/ST favourite and launched one of Britain’s best-known late-’80s platform heroes.

Rick Dangerous 2.history: Rick Dangerous 2 (also styled Rick Dangerous II) is Core Design’s 1990 sequel, released on Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, CPC and related platforms. The adventurer faces new themed worlds packed with traps, enemies and inventively cruel puzzles. It refined the series’ demanding platform craft and remained a staple of European 16-bit platform catalogues into the early 1990s.

Risky Woods.history: Risky Woods is a 1992 action-platformer by Dinamic and Zeus Software, published by Electronic Arts on Amiga, Atari ST and PC. A warrior battles through dark fantasy stages with fluid combat and bold graphics. As a Spanish-developed EA release it brought arcade-style hack-and-slash spectacle to late Amiga and ST audiences hungry for console-like action.

Roadwar 2000.history: Roadwar 2000 is Strategic Simulations’ 1986 post-apocalyptic strategy game for Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST and other computers. Players lead a gang across a ruined America, recruiting vehicles and fighting for scarce resources on a strategic map. It brought SSI’s wargame sensibility to Mad Max–style road warfare and was a distinctive C64/Amiga strategy cult title.

Roadwar Europa.history: Roadwar Europa is SSI’s 1987 sequel to Roadwar 2000, appearing on Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST and related systems. The vehicular gang warfare shifts to a devastated Europe with new maps, factions and campaign challenges. It extended SSI’s post-holocaust strategy niche on 8- and 16-bit machines for players who wanted turn-based conquest with cars and scavenged firepower.

Roadwars.history: Roadwars is a 1987 futuristic combat racer by Arcadia Systems / Melbourne House for Amiga, Atari ST and Commodore 64. Two players (or one against the computer) battle along a tunnel roadway, shooting and colliding to eliminate the rival craft. Its dual-play 3D corridor action was an early Amiga showcase of smooth vector-style combat racing.

Robocop.history: Robocop is Ocean Software’s hugely successful late-1980s film licence, converted across Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, CPC, Spectrum and more. Side-scrolling shooting, platform sections and set pieces recreate the cyborg cop’s Detroit crusade. On British 8-bit machines it was a chart-dominating Ocean blockbuster and one of the most recognisable movie games of the period.

Robocop 2.history: Robocop 2 is Ocean’s early-1990s follow-up licence to the second RoboCop film, released on Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and other formats. Action stages again cast players as the cybernetic officer battling crime with heavy weaponry and platform challenges. It continued Ocean’s film-tie-in pipeline on Amiga and 8-bit shelves when licensed action games remained a commercial mainstay.

Rocket Ranger.history: Rocket Ranger is Cinemaware’s 1988 interactive movie-style adventure for Amiga, Commodore 64, Atari ST and other systems. A rocket-packed hero fights a pulp World War II alternate history, mixing strategy maps, flight sequences and fistfights. Lavish presentation made it a flagship Amiga Cinemaware title and a showcase for cinematic storytelling on 16-bit home computers.

Rod-Land.history: Rod-Land is Jaleco’s cute 1990 arcade platformer, ported to Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and Amstrad CPC. Twin fairy sisters clear single-screen rooms by stunning monsters with magic rods and slamming them into the ground. Cheerful visuals and co-op charm made the home conversions popular European Amiga/ST arcade ports in the early 1990s.

Rodland.history: Rodland is the compact spelling of Jaleco’s Rod-Land, the fairy-sister arcade platformer widely converted to Amiga, Atari ST, C64 and CPC around 1990–91. Players stun and thrash enemies across brightly coloured single-screen stages, often in two-player mode. It became a staple cute’em-up conversion on European 16-bit machines and a favourite of early-’90s magazine coverdisks and compilations.

Rogue.history: Rogue is the seminal early-1980s dungeon crawler by Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold that defined the roguelike genre. Exploring procedurally generated ASCII (and later tiled) labyrinths, players fight monsters, gather loot and face permadeath. Ports and clones reached Commodore and other home computers, spreading turn-based dungeon adventure far beyond university mainframes into Amiga/ST-era freeware culture.

Roland in Space.history: Roland in Space is an Amstrad CPC platform-adventure starring Amstrad’s soft mascot Roland, published in the mid-1980s for the CPC range. The character explores space-themed screens collecting items and avoiding hazards in simple cartoon levels. As part of Amstrad’s early first-party/affiliate software push, it helped give the CPC a recognisable on-screen hero for new computer owners.

Roland in Time.history: Roland in Time is a mid-1980s Amstrad CPC platform game featuring the Roland mascot travelling across historical periods. Players jump through themed eras collecting objects and dodging period hazards in accessible levels aimed at home users. Together with other Roland titles, it anchored Amstrad’s effort to brand the CPC with friendly, machine-exclusive character software.

Rubicon.history: Rubicon is a 1992 Amiga horizontal shoot-’em-up developed by Century Interactive and published by 21st Century Entertainment. A lone fighter blasts through post-nuclear stages with power-ups and large end guardians. Arriving in the Amiga’s rich shmup years, it offered solid arcade action and is remembered among European disk-based shooters of the early 1990s.

Saboteur II.history: Saboteur II (Avenging Angel) is Durell Software’s 1987 sequel to Saboteur, released on ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Amstrad CPC. Playing as the original ninja’s sister, you infiltrate a sprawling fortress with combat, exploration and timed objectives. Larger maps and stronger adventure elements made it a standout British 8-bit stealth-action title of the late 1980s.

Saboteur!.history: Saboteur! is Durell’s 1985 stealth-action classic for ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Amstrad CPC. As a black-clad infiltrator you sneak through a warehouse complex, planting explosives and avoiding guards with careful timing. Its tense atmosphere and open-feeling map made it a landmark Spectrum/CPC favourite and a precursor to later stealth games on home micros.

Sacred Armour of Antiriad.history: The Sacred Armour of Antiriad is Palace Software’s 1986 post-apocalyptic adventure-platformer for Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum, Amstrad CPC and other systems. A lone hero seeks a legendary powered suit across ruined landscapes blending exploration, puzzles and combat. Distinctive art and comic-book framing made it a memorable mid-’80s British 8-bit release from the Palace catalogue.

Sam's Journey.history: Sam’s Journey is a modern Commodore 64 platform adventure released in 2017 by Protovision, designed as new commercial software for the classic machine rather than a period original. Polished scrolling levels, contemporary design standards and physical boxed editions showcased what today’s C64 homebrew can achieve. It stands as a flagship 2010s revival title for the living Commodore scene.

Sanxion.history: Sanxion is a 1986 Commodore 64 horizontal shoot-’em-up by Stavros Fasoulas, published by Thalamus. Dual-viewpoint blasting and relentless waves made it a polished mid-’80s C64 shmup, while Rob Hubbard’s loading music became one of the SID chip’s most famous pieces. It helped establish Thalamus’s reputation and remains as celebrated for its soundtrack as for its action.

Sapiens.history: Sapiens is a mid-1980s prehistoric survival adventure from French publisher Loriciels, known especially on Amstrad CPC and other European micros. Players hunt, craft and endure in a Stone Age world that emphasises exploration and resourcefulness over arcade reflexes. It reflected the CPC’s strong French adventure catalogue and offered a distinctive anthropological theme uncommon in contemporary action games.

Savage.history: Savage is a 1988 action game by Probe Software, published by Firebird for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, CPC and Spectrum. It packs three distinct styles—side-scrolling combat, pseudo-3D corridor blasting and a creature-control finale—into one package. Bold graphics and David Whittaker’s audio made it a flashy multi-load showcase on late-’80s European home computers.

Scarabaeus.history: Scarabaeus is a mid-1980s Commodore 64 adventure by Andromeda Software, set in an Egyptian tomb of mazes, puzzles and first-person exploration. Players navigate shifting corridors, decode secrets and avoid deadly traps in search of ancient treasure. Atmospheric presentation made it a distinctive C64 adventure and a favourite among players seeking something moodier than standard platform fare.

SDI - Strategic Defence Initiative.history: SDI – Strategic Defence Initiative is Sega’s mid-1980s arcade missile-defence shooter, converted for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and other homes under Activision and partners. Players rotate a satellite weapon to destroy incoming warheads and enemy craft before they strike. Cold War theming and coin-op spectacle made the ports a timely Amiga/ST arcade conversion when space-defence games were headline material.

Second Samurai.history: Second Samurai is Vivid Image’s 1994 Amiga action-platformer (also on other late formats), sequel in spirit to First Samurai. A warrior battles through lush levels combining combat, puzzles and cinematic set pieces with strong sound and animation. It arrived as a late flagship Amiga platformer, showing the machine could still deliver premium action as console competition intensified.

Sensible Soccer.history: Sensible Soccer is Sensible Software’s landmark early-1990s football game, exploding onto Amiga and Atari ST before wider ports. Tiny sprites, huge pitches, blistering pace and sharp AI made it the definitive European computer soccer experience for many players. Magazines crowned it endlessly; on the Amiga it became cultural shorthand for the platform’s sporting golden age.

Sensible World of Soccer.history: Sensible World of Soccer (SWOS) is Sensible Software’s mid-1990s expansion of Sensible Soccer for Amiga and PC, adding vast career, transfer and world-database depth. The famous overhead action remained, now wrapped in management systems that kept players hooked for seasons. It is widely regarded as one of the Amiga’s greatest sports games and a high point of British game design.

Sensible World of Soccer '95/'96.history: Sensible World of Soccer ’95/’96 is an updated Amiga/PC edition of Sensible’s football opus with refreshed squads and data for the 1995–96 season. It keeps the classic micro-sprite matches and deep career tools that defined SWOS. For Amiga football fans, seasonal updates prolonged the life of the platform’s most important soccer franchise.

Sensible World of Soccer '96/'97.history: Sensible World of Soccer ’96/’97 continues Sensible Software’s Amiga and PC football series with squad and competition updates for the 1996–97 season. On-pitch play stays true to the ultra-fast Sensible formula while career and transfer systems remain central. It was among the last major seasonal SWOS refreshes cherished by the late Amiga football community.

Sensible World of Soccer v1.1.history: Sensible World of Soccer v1.1 is a revised release of Sensible Software’s mid-1990s Amiga/PC football megagame, tightening bugs and data after the original SWOS launch. The blend of arcade matches and encyclopedic career mode that made the series legendary remains intact. Versioned updates mattered on Amiga because the game became a living platform for competitive and managerial play.

Sentinel Worlds I: Future Magic.history: Sentinel Worlds I: Future Magic is a 1988 science-fiction role-playing game by Paul Reiche III, published by Electronic Arts for PC and later home systems including Commodore-era catalogues. Crewing a spaceship, players explore planets, talk to NPCs and fight in both ground and space combat. Open-ended EA sci-fi RPG design made it a notable late-’80s alternative to pure dungeon crawlers on personal computers.

Shadow of the Beast.history: Reflections Interactive developed Shadow of the Beast for Psygnosis, releasing it on the Amiga in 1989 before Atari ST and other ports followed. A side-scrolling action-adventure with grotesque fantasy art, multilayer parallax and a David Whittaker score, it was sold as much as a hardware showcase as a game. On 16-bit machines—especially the Amiga—it became a defining late-80s “look what this box can do” title and a flagship of Psygnosis’s glossy European catalogue.

Shadow of the Beast II.history: Shadow of the Beast II arrived in 1990 as Reflections and Psygnosis’s Amiga sequel, with Atari ST and later console versions following. It kept the series’ dark fantasy setting and cinematic presentation while leaning harder into adventure, inventory puzzles and non-linear exploration. On Amiga shelves it confirmed Beast as a prestige franchise and remained a frequent demo-disk and magazine cover star for its atmosphere and Tim Follin / Geoff Follin soundtrack work.

Shadow of the Beast III.history: Shadow of the Beast III: Out of the Shadow closed the Amiga trilogy in 1992, again from Reflections under the Psygnosis label. It shifted toward more conventional platform-action pacing while retaining the series’ ornate visuals and orchestral-leaning game music. As a late OCS-era Psygnosis release it mattered less as a technical bombshell than as the finale of one of the Amiga’s most recognisable fantasy brands.

Shinobi.history: Sega’s Shinobi hit arcades in 1987 as a side-scrolling ninja action game built around precise shuriken combat, hostage rescues and boss fights. Home computer ports by The Edge and others reached Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum in the late 1980s. Though the micros trimmed arcade spectacle, the conversions still brought a major Sega brand into European computer shops and helped popularise ninja run-and-gun gameplay on 8- and 16-bit machines.

Shockway Rider.history: Shockway Rider is a 1987 Faster Than Light / Gargoyle Games title for Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum. Players dash along a futuristic moving walkway, dodging and punching through waves of urban thugs in a sideways-scrolling brawler framed as a deadly commute. It stood out on 8-bit machines for its oddball concept and slick Gargoyle presentation more than for longevity, a cult curiosity of the mid-price UK software boom.

Shufflepuck Cafe.history: Shufflepuck Café is an air-hockey sports game by Broderbund, released in the late 1980s for Macintosh and soon ported to Amiga, Atari ST and other platforms. You face a roster of eccentric alien opponents across a table, learning each rival’s timing and dirty tricks. On 16-bit European computers it became a favourite two-player and versus-AI diversion—simple to grasp, highly replayable, and memorable for its character-driven challenge ladder.

Shufflepuck Café.history: Shufflepuck Café is Broderbund’s late-1980s air-hockey game, first known on Macintosh and widely played on Amiga and Atari ST ports. Matches pit you against a gallery of quirky alien regulars, each with distinct serving styles and temperaments. It mattered on 16-bit micros as a pure versus sports toy: short rounds, strong personality, and endless “one more game” duels that suited living-room and office machines alike.

Shuttle.history: Shuttle: The Space Flight Simulator was developed by Vektor Grafix and published by Virgin Games around 1992 for Amiga, Atari ST and PC. It attempted a serious recreation of NASA Space Shuttle procedures, from launch and orbital operations to landing, with dense instrumentation and mission briefings. On Amiga and ST it stood apart from arcade space shooters as a patient, systems-heavy sim aimed at players who wanted cockpit authenticity over twitch action.

Sigma 7.history: Sigma 7 is a 1986–1987 Durell Software multi-stage action game for Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and related formats. It chains shoot-em-up, maze and puzzle-tinged sections into one budget-friendly cassette epic typical of mid-80s UK software houses. On 8-bit machines it is remembered as a solid Durell package rather than a genre landmark—an example of how British publishers mixed arcade styles to fill a single tape.

Silent Service.history: MicroProse’s Silent Service, designed by Sid Meier and released in 1985, is a World War II submarine simulation that spread across Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST, PC and other platforms. Players plot patrols in the Pacific, manage torpedo attacks and dive to avoid destroyers. It helped establish MicroProse’s reputation for accessible yet meaty military sims and remained a staple of serious strategy/sim libraries on both 8-bit and 16-bit home computers.

Silkworm.history: Tecmo’s Silkworm arcade game (1988) is a horizontally scrolling shoot-em-up where one player flies a helicopter and another drives an armed jeep. The Sales Curve / Random Access home conversions brought it to Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, CPC and Spectrum with surprising fidelity. On European micros—especially Amiga and ST—it became a co-op favourite and a benchmark for how good a late-80s arcade shmup port could feel.

Sim City.history: Will Wright and Maxis launched SimCity in 1989, with versions quickly reaching Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and other home computers after its initial PC success. Players zone land, balance budgets and watch a city grow—or collapse—without a fixed win state. On Amiga and ST it popularised the “software toy” city-builder and proved open-ended simulation could be a mainstream hit beside arcade and adventure genres.

Simon the Sorcerer.history: Adventure Soft’s Simon the Sorcerer debuted in 1993 as a point-and-click comedy adventure, with prominent Amiga and PC releases (plus later formats). Written with a Monty Python–tinged British humour, it follows a teenager dropped into a fairy-tale world of sarcastic dialogue and inventory puzzles. On the Amiga it stood among the early-90s adventure wave that kept the platform competitive with PC CD-ROM storytelling.

Simon the Sorcerer (AGA).history: The AGA Amiga edition of Adventure Soft’s Simon the Sorcerer (1993) takes advantage of newer Amiga graphics chipsets for richer colour and presentation while keeping the same point-and-click comedy adventure. Simon’s snarky fairy-tale quest was a highlight of mid-90s Amiga adventure gaming, and the AGA version showcased how 32-bit Amigas could host talkie-era style adventures closer to contemporary PC releases.

Skate or Die!.history: Electronic Arts released Skate or Die! in 1987 as a freestyle skateboarding sports compilation, famously strong on the Commodore 64 and also appearing on other late-80s platforms. Events range from half-pipe tricks to downhill races and pool jams, wrapped in EA’s loud California attitude. On the C64 it became one of the era’s defining skate-culture games and a showcase for personality-driven sports multi-events.

Skweek.history: Skweek (also known as Schwartzkopf in some territories) is a 1989 Loriciel puzzle-action game originally big on Atari ST and Amiga, with other home computer versions following. You roll a small creature across tile grids, flipping colours while avoiding enemies and hazards. Its cute presentation and tidy level design made it a familiar European puzzle staple and the seed of Loriciel’s later Super Skweek sequels.

Slam Tilt.history: Slam Tilt is a 1996 Amiga pinball package from 21st Century Entertainment, creators of the Pinball Dreams lineage. It offers multiple richly themed tables with multiball, ramps and the polished physics Amiga pinball fans expected by the mid-90s. Coming late in the Amiga’s commercial life, it still mattered as proof the platform remained a pinball powerhouse when many other genres had migrated to PC.

Slap Fight.history: Slap Fight (known as Alcon in some regions) is a 1986 Toaplan vertical shoot-em-up that reached arcades before home ports on Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and other systems. Its defining twist is a shop-style power-up menu that lets you buy speed, weapons and options mid-run. Computer conversions kept that upgrade fantasy alive for European shmup fans who wanted a Toaplan-style vertical blast on living-room micros.

Sleepwalker.history: Sleepwalker is a 1993 Ocean Software platform game released for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and other formats as an official Comic Relief charity title starring the Sleepwalker character and sidekick Sid. Players guide hazards away from the sleepwalking hero rather than controlling him directly. It is remembered on Amiga and 8-bit machines both as a clever twist on platforming and as a high-profile fundraising crossover with British TV comedy culture.

Snowstrike.history: Snowstrike (also styled Snow Strike) is a late-1980s combat flight game from Epyx and U.S. Gold, appearing on Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST, CPC, Spectrum and PC around 1989–1990. Players fly an F-14-style fighter on anti-drug cartel missions over Colombia, mixing bombing runs with dogfights. It never rivalled MicroProse’s top sims in acclaim, but it was a typical big-box action flyer on European 8- and 16-bit shelves.

Solomon's Key.history: Tecmo’s Solomon’s Key began in arcades in 1986 as a room-by-room puzzle platformer about creating and breaking blocks to reach a key and exit. Home versions followed on Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, Atari ST, Amiga and other platforms. On European micros it stood out for brainy, timing-sensitive level design rather than pure action, and it helped popularise block-creation puzzle platforming long before later clones.

Sonic the Hedgehog.history: Sega’s Sonic the Hedgehog launched on the Mega Drive/Genesis in 1991, defining 16-bit platform speed with loops, springboards and the attitude-heavy mascot that challenged Mario. Official Western ports targeted consoles more than Amiga or ST, yet the character and unofficial computer conversions still flooded European demo culture and coverdisk chatter. For retro libraries it remains the landmark blue-hedgehog platformer of the early 1990s console wars.

Sorcery+.history: Sorcery+ is Virgin Games’ enhanced 1985–1986 edition of the flip-screen adventure Sorcery, created as a showcase for the Amstrad CPC (with related versions elsewhere). Players guide a sorcerer across haunted landscapes collecting objects and casting spells. On the CPC it mattered as a glossy first-party-style demonstration of colour and animation, often cited among the machine’s early must-play British adventure-action titles.

Soul Force.history: Soul Force is a modern Commodore 64 homebrew horizontal shoot-em-up by Sarah Jane Avory, published by Protovision in 2020. Built in 6502 assembly with dozens of themed stages, bosses and upgradeable weapons, it deliberately echoes Gradius- and R-Type-style arcade structure. Clearly labelled as contemporary C64 software, it earned strong praise in the homebrew scene—including major community awards—and showed new commercial shmups could still thrill on the machine.

Space Rogue.history: Origin Systems released Space Rogue in 1989 as a hybrid space-adventure game for platforms including Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST and PC. It mixes first-person space combat and trading with docking at ships where top-down adventure sections unfold. Coming from the Ultima studio, it mattered on late 8-bit and 16-bit computers as an ambitious bridge between Elite-like flight and RPG storytelling.

Space Taxi.history: Space Taxi is a 1984 Commodore 64 action game by John Kutcher, published by Muse Software. You pilot a thrust-based taxi between landing pads, ferrying passengers while managing fuel and brutal inertia physics across themed floors. Its digitized speech (“hey taxi”) and merciless landing challenge made it a C64 classic and a frequent reference point for later pad-landing and private-hire parody games.

Special Forces.history: MicroProse’s Special Forces (1991) is a squad-based tactical action sequel spirit to Airborne Ranger, released for Amiga, Atari ST and PC. Players plan loadouts then control commandos through infiltration missions with stealth, firefights and objectives behind enemy lines. On 16-bit machines it extended MicroProse’s military action line into small-unit tactics for fans who wanted more than a lone-wolf arcade raid.

Speedball.history: The Bitmap Brothers’ Speedball launched in 1988 on Amiga and Atari ST (with later ports) as a violent futuristic sports game published by Image Works. Two teams batter each other across a metal arena to score with a steel ball, spending coins on brutal upgrades. Its industrial art style and freeze-frame violence made it an instant 16-bit cult hit and the foundation of one of the Amiga’s great sports franchises.

Speedball 2.history: Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe (1990) is the Bitmap Brothers’ landmark Amiga and Atari ST sequel, later widely ported. It enlarges the cyberpunk sport with transfers, a deeper shop, tighter arena flow and the chant-along rock soundtrack fans still quote. On European 16-bit computers it became the definitive futuristic sports title—endlessly replayable in two-player and a cornerstone of the Bitmap Brothers’ reputation.

Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe.history: Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe, released in 1990 by the Bitmap Brothers and Image Works, refined the original’s savage future sport for Amiga, Atari ST and numerous later platforms. Managerial upgrades, brutal tackles and goal-mouth chaos made every match a spectacle. It is widely regarded as one of the Amiga’s finest multiplayer games and the series’ creative peak.

Speedball II - Brutal Deluxe.history: Speedball II – Brutal Deluxe is the same 1990 Bitmap Brothers sequel known more commonly as Speedball 2, a futuristic arena sport hit on Amiga and Atari ST before broad ports. Teams buy armour and weapons, thrash rivals and chase high scores in steel stadiums. Under any spelling it remains a defining 16-bit sports-action classic of the early 1990s.

Spellbound.history: Spellbound (1985) is David Jones’s Magic Knight adventure for Mastertronic, released on Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and related machines. Combining arcade adventure exploration with character commands and inventory puzzles, it deepened the Magic Knight formula begun in Finders Keepers. As a cheap yet ambitious 8-bit title it showed budget labels could ship sophisticated adventure systems, not only disposable arcade clones.

Spindizzy.history: Spindizzy is a 1986 Electric Dreams isometric action-puzzle game by Paul Shirley, famous on Amstrad CPC, Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum and later 16-bit ports. You remotely steer the Territorial Acquisition of Habiforming Devices And Reconnaissance craft—a spinning top—across treacherous maps to map and claim territory. Its Marble Madness–adjacent physics and elegant maps made it a critical darling of mid-80s British software.

SRAM.history: SRAM is a mid-1980s French graphic adventure by ERE Informatique, closely associated with the Amstrad CPC and also seen on other European micros. Players explore a post-apocalyptic world with a text/icon-driven interface typical of French adventure design of the period. It mattered especially on the CPC scene as an early showcase of ambitious local storytelling before the better-known sequel expanded the setting.

SRAM 2.history: SRAM 2 continues ERE Informatique’s French post-apocalyptic adventure series for Amstrad CPC and related late-80s machines. It builds on the first game’s exploration and puzzle structure with a larger scenario and the same distinctive Gallic adventure presentation. For CPC owners it was a substantial follow-up from a key French studio that also helped shape European adventure expectations before Cryo-era successors.

Star Paws.history: Star Paws is a 1987 Software Projects action game for Commodore 64 (with other versions), designed around herding and blasting rogue space creatures in a surreal ranch setting. It is especially prized for Rob Hubbard’s soundtrack, which became a SID-scene favourite independent of the quirky gameplay. On the C64 it endures as a music-first cult title from the Software Projects catalogue.

Star Wars.history: Domark’s late-1980s home conversions of Atari’s Star Wars arcade machine brought vector-style trench runs, tie-fighter battles and Death Star assaults to Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, CPC and Spectrum. Though home hardware softened the arcade’s vector crispness, the licensed fantasy still sold widely. On European micros it was one of the most recognisable film-tie-in shooters of the era and a staple of Christmas compilations.

Stardust.history: Stardust is a 1993 Amiga shoot-em-up by Finnish studio Bloodhouse, later followed by related titles such as Super Stardust. It wraps Asteroids-like free-roaming combat in hand-drawn tunnels, bosses and a heavy techno soundtrack. On AGA and OCS Amigas it became a late-era showcase of Finnish coding flair and helped Bloodhouse / Housemarque build the reputation that carried into later console hits.

Starglider.history: Starglider (1986) is Argonaut Software’s 3D shoot-em-up published by Rainbird for Amiga, Atari ST, and earlier for other formats including 8-bit machines. Piloting a wireframe/filled craft across a defended planet, players dogfight and complete ground attacks with a memorable digital title theme on 16-bit versions. It was a flagship Rainbird release that advertised what fast 3D action could look like on ST and Amiga.

Starglider 2.history: Starglider 2: The Egrons Strike Back arrived in 1988 from Argonaut and Rainbird as a fuller 3D sequel on Amiga, Atari ST and PC. It expands planetary flight into trading, exploration and larger-scale war against the Egrons, with solid-filled graphics that pushed 16-bit machines. It mattered as a bridge between arcade space combat and open 3D worlds, cementing Argonaut’s pre-Super FX reputation.

Steel Ranger.history: Steel Ranger is a modern Commodore 64 homebrew action-adventure released in 2018 by Covert BitOps (Lasse Öörni) and published by Psytronik. Inspired by Turrican and Metroid, it sends a cybernetic ranger through a huge scrolling world of upgrades, exploration and bosses. Explicitly a contemporary C64 commercial release—not a 1980s original—it became one of the most acclaimed recent games on the platform and a flagship of the homebrew revival.

Stormlord.history: Stormlord is a 1989 Hewson Consultants platform-adventure by Raffaele Cecco, released on Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, CPC and Spectrum. Players rescue fairy-like captives across ornate, trap-filled levels with Cecco’s trademark precision design. On 8- and 16-bit European machines it continued the designer’s run of highly polished action-adventures and is still cited for its graphics and demanding set-pieces.

Strike Fleet.history: Strike Fleet (1987) is a naval combat simulation from Lucasfilm Games / Electronic Arts, with versions for Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST and other platforms. Commanding modern warships, players manage fleets through Cold War–flavoured scenarios involving missiles, aircraft and task-force tactics. It brought a more approachable real-time naval war experience to home computers beside denser keyboard-driven sims.

Stunt Car Racer.history: Geoff Crammond’s Stunt Car Racer (also Stunt Track Racer) launched in 1989 via MicroStyle/MicroProse on Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and other formats. Drivers race turbocharged cars on elevated roller-coaster tracks where jumps and crashes are part of the contest. Its convincing 3D physics made it a landmark racer on 16-bit machines and a lasting favourite for two-player link-up duels.

Summer Games.history: Epyx’s Summer Games (1984) set the template for Olympic multi-event sports on Commodore 64 and other mid-80s computers, later influencing Amiga/ST-era sequels. Players compete in diving, running, swimming and more with joystick-timed techniques and medal ceremonies. On the C64 especially it became a party staple and the foundation of Epyx’s long Games series that defined sports compilations on home micros.

Summer Games II.history: Summer Games II followed in 1985 from Epyx, expanding the Olympic multi-sports formula on Commodore 64 and related platforms with new events such as fencing, cycling and kayaking. Shared records, opening ceremonies and hot-seat multiplayer kept it central to living-room competition. Together with the first game it cemented Epyx’s dominance of 8-bit athletic compilations before Winter and World Games continued the brand.

Super Boulder Dash.history: Super Boulder Dash is a mid-1980s compilation pairing First Star Software’s Boulder Dash with Boulder Dash II, widely sold on Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and other systems. The cave-digging, rock-dropping puzzle-action formula—collect jewels, avoid monsters, outthink physics—was already iconic; bundling both games made it an easy entry point. On European 8-bit machines it kept Push-Push diamond hunting in constant rotation at budget prices.

Super Cars.history: Super Cars is a 1990 Gremlin Graphics top-down racing-combat game for Amiga, Atari ST and other formats, developed with the style later associated with Magnetic Fields. Players win purse money, buy weapon and armour upgrades, and battle through a season of arena-like tracks. It helped establish the shop-and-race loop that Super Cars II and related Gremlin racers refined for 16-bit audiences.

Super Cars II.history: Super Cars II (1991) is Gremlin’s Amiga and Atari ST sequel that enlarges the top-down combat racing season with more tracks, weapons and championship structure. Its crisp presentation and upgrade economy made it a favourite alternative to sprite-scaling racers like Lotus. On 16-bit European machines it stands as one of the stronger overhead racers of the early 1990s.

Super Mario Bros. 64.history: Super Mario 64 (often casually called Super Mario Bros. 64) launched with the Nintendo 64 in 1996 as Nintendo’s pioneering 3D platformer. Mario explores open courses from Princess Peach’s castle, collecting Power Stars via analog-stick acrobatics that redefined camera and movement design. Though not an Amiga/ST contemporary, it is the landmark mid-90s console title that set the template every later 3D platformer answered to.

Super Skweek.history: Super Skweek is Loriciel’s early-1990s sequel to Skweek, prominent on Amiga, Atari ST and other European computers. The colourful tile-flipping action expands with more enemies, power-ups and larger stage sets while keeping the cute rolling-hero fantasy. It kept Loriciel’s puzzle-action brand visible on 16-bit shelves and remains the best-known follow-up for fans of the original Skweek loop.

Superfrog.history: Team17’s Superfrog hopped onto the Amiga in 1993 as a bright, high-speed platformer about a prince cursed into frog form. Packed with secret routes, set-piece levels and a memorable soundtrack, it showcased Team17’s arcade polish beyond Alien Breed. On AGA and OCS Amigas it became one of the platform’s classic cute’em-up mascot games of the mid-1990s.

Supremacy.history: Supremacy (released as Overlord in North America) is a 1990 strategy game by Probe Software and Virgin, available on Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and other systems. Players manage planetary economies and fleets in a cold war of expansion against an AI opponent. On 16-bit machines it offered a more approachable 4X-lite empire struggle and stood out for its slick presentation among early-90s space strategy titles.

Switchblade.history: Switchblade is a 1989 Gremlin Graphics action-platformer designed by Core Design talent, released on Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, CPC and Spectrum. Descendants explore a ruined tower, assembling a broken fireblade while fighting mutants in a bleak, atmospheric setting. It mattered as an early Core-style exploratory platformer and set up the better-known Amiga sequel.

Switchblade II.history: Switchblade II arrived in 1991 on the Amiga (with other versions) as Core Design and Gremlin’s louder, chunkier follow-up to the original exploratory platformer. Bigger weapons, smoother scrolling and comic-book visuals pushed it toward run-and-gun territory while keeping underground exploration. It is often ranked among the Amiga’s standout early-90s action platformers.

Swiv.history: SWIV (often written Swiv) is a 1991 vertically scrolling shoot-em-up by The Sales Curve / Random Access, spiritual successor thinking to Silkworm, for Amiga, Atari ST and home computer ports. One player flies a helicopter while another drives an armed jeep through relentless enemy waves. On European 16-bit machines it became a co-op shmup benchmark and a staple of early-90s action collections.

SWIV.history: SWIV is The Sales Curve’s 1991 vertical co-op shoot-em-up for Amiga, Atari ST and other formats, born from the team behind the Silkworm conversions. Helicopter and jeep partners blast through densely authored stages packed with ground and air targets. Under the all-caps title it is the same defining early-90s micro shmup still cited whenever Amiga shoot-em-ups are ranked.

Syndicate.history: Bullfrog Productions’ Syndicate (1993), published by Electronic Arts, is a dystopian real-time tactics game iconic on Amiga and PC. Players control chip-implanted agents through isometric cities, assassinating targets and conquering territories for a mega-corporation. Its bleak cyberpunk tone and squad control influenced countless tactics games and remains one of the Amiga’s late classic strategy-action landmarks.

Target Renegade.history: Target Renegade is Imagine/Ocean’s 1988 sequel to Renegade for Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and later conversions. A side-scrolling beat-em-up about clearing streets and car parks of gang enemies, it tightened combat and multi-plane brawling for 8-bit hardware. On UK micros it was one of the strongest home follow-ups to the arcade Kunio-kun / Renegade boom.

Target: Renegade.history: Target: Renegade (1988) is the Ocean/Imagine beat-em-up sequel to Renegade, widely played on Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum. You fight through multi-load stages of street gangs to rescue a kidnapped relative, using pipes, bikes and raw brawling. Colon-title listings refer to the same influential UK 8-bit brawler that kept the Renegade franchise alive beyond the arcade original.

Techno Cop.history: Techno Cop is a 1988 action hybrid developed by Gray Matter and Imagexcel and published in Europe by Gremlin Graphics. Versions reached Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and other formats. Players alternate Out Run–style pursuit driving with side-scrolling building raids as a futuristic lawman. Violent for its day and musically remembered for Ben Daglish’s score, it was a typical late-80s Gremlin package title bridging road combat and run-and-gun on European micros.

Terry's Big Adventure.history: Terry's Big Adventure is a 1989 side-scrolling platformer by Gametec, published by Shades Software and Grandslam for Commodore 64, Amiga and Atari ST. Players guide Terry through colourful levels armed mainly with a yo-yo, bouncing and battling across a dozen stages. An early Allister Brimble credit on the C64, it sat in the cute-platformer wave of the late 8- and 16-bit era without becoming a major franchise hit.

Tetris.history: Alexey Pajitnov created Tetris in the mid-1980s in the Soviet Union; Western home-computer editions followed via Mirrorsoft, Spectrum HoloByte and others on Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST, Amstrad CPC and more. Falling tetrominoes, line clears and rising pace made it an instant abstract classic. On European micros it proved that a pure puzzle idea could dominate charts alongside arcade conversions and helped cement Tetris as a universal language of play.

Thanatos.history: Thanatos is a 1986 side-view adventure-action game by Durell Software for ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Amstrad CPC. You control a huge dragon flying across a continuous landscape, breathing fire, snatching people and searching for a magical artefact. Unusual scale and atmosphere set it apart from standard shooters; on 8-bit machines it remains a cult Durell title remembered for its bold fantasy premise and fluid scrolling.

The Bard's Tale - Tales of the Unknown.history: Tales of the Unknown: The Bard's Tale, developed by Interplay and published by Electronic Arts in 1985, brought party-based dungeon crawling to Apple II and then Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST and other platforms. Exploring Skara Brae’s streets and multi-level mazes with a bard-led party, it offered colourful first-person views and memorable magic. On home computers it became one of the defining mid-80s CRPGs and launched a long-running series.

The Bard's Tale: Tales of the Unknown.history: Interplay’s The Bard's Tale (full title Tales of the Unknown) arrived in 1985 from Electronic Arts as a first-person party RPG. Ports to Commodore 64, Amiga and Atari ST carried its city-and-dungeon crawl, witty magic system and colourful wireframe-to-bitmap presentation across European 8- and 16-bit machines. It mattered as a more approachable rival to Ultima-style epics and as the foundation of Interplay’s best-known fantasy franchise.

The Chaos Engine.history: The Chaos Engine is a 1993 top-down steampunk run-and-gun by The Bitmap Brothers, published by Renegade for Amiga and Atari ST (with later ports). One or two players pick Victorian-sci-fi mercenaries and blast through maze-like levels packed with monsters and upgrades. Tight co-op, distinctive art and a thumping soundtrack made it a flagship Bitmap Brothers title and a late golden-age Amiga multiplayer staple.

The Chaos Engine (AGA).history: The Chaos Engine’s AGA Amiga editions sharpen The Bitmap Brothers’ 1993 steampunk co-op shooter with richer palettes on Amiga 1200-class machines. The core remains frantic top-down blasting through industrial fantasy maps with selectable characters and shared firepower. On AGA hardware it showed how a Renegade/Bitmap classic could look even denser without losing the tight two-player action that defined the original OCS hit.

The Eidolon.history: The Eidolon is a 1985 first-person adventure from Lucasfilm Games, published by Epyx and Activision on Commodore 64, Atari 8-bit and later Amstrad CPC and other formats. Using fractal-generated tunnels, players ride a mysterious vehicle through caverns collecting jewels and facing creatures. It showcased Lucasfilm’s experimental 3D look on 8-bit machines and stands with Rescue on Fractalus as an early home-computer VR-style fantasy.

The Great Giana Sisters.history: The Great Giana Sisters, developed by Time Warp and published by Rainbow Arts in 1987, is a side-scrolling platformer for Commodore 64, Amiga and Atari ST. Its Mario-like structure—blocks, power-ups and whimsical levels—sparked legal pressure that quickly pulled it from many shelves. Scarcity and Chris Hülsbeck’s iconic SID theme turned it into a legend of the C64 and early Amiga scene, remembered as much for controversy as for play.

The Guild of Thieves.history: The Guild of Thieves is a 1987 illustrated text adventure by Magnetic Scrolls, published by Rainbird for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and other systems. Set in the fantasy land of Kerovnia, it tasks would-be thieves with a grand burglary scored on loot value. Following The Pawn, it cemented Magnetic Scrolls as Rainbird’s prestige adventure house and a stylish rival to Infocom on 16-bit European machines.

The Hobbit.history: Melbourne House’s The Hobbit (1982), based on Tolkien’s novel, was a groundbreaking illustrated text adventure for ZX Spectrum that spread to Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, BBC Micro and beyond. Its parser, timed events and semi-independent characters made Middle-earth feel alive compared with static treasure hunts. Hugely popular in Europe, it proved licensed literary fantasy could drive home-computer adventure sales and influenced later graphic adventures.

The Last Ninja.history: System 3’s The Last Ninja landed on the Commodore 64 in 1987, with Amiga, Atari ST and other ports following. Isometric martial-arts adventure stages send a lone ninja through weapons puzzles, combat and exploration across richly drawn levels. A C64 showcase for graphics and sound, it became one of System 3’s defining hits and a cornerstone of late-80s 8-bit action-adventure design.

The Legend of Blacksilver.history: The Legend of Blacksilver is a 1988 role-playing game from Epyx for Commodore 64 and Apple II, often treated as a spiritual follow-up to Legacy of the Ancients. Players explore towns, wilds and dungeons in a quest involving the magical metal blacksilver. On the C64 it offered a more streamlined Epyx RPG experience and remains a niche entry in the late golden age of 8-bit computer role-playing.

The Lost Patrol.history: The Lost Patrol is a 1990 Vietnam War game by Shadow Development, published by Ocean for Amiga and Atari ST. After a helicopter crash, you lead survivors across hostile territory through strategy map moves, tense firefights and interactive sequences. Bleak tone and moral pressure made it stand out from Ocean’s arcade licences; on the Amiga it is remembered as an ambitious, uneasy war narrative rather than pure action.

The Magic Candle.history: Mindcraft’s The Magic Candle (1989) is a party-based fantasy RPG released for Commodore 64, Apple II, MS-DOS and later other formats. Heroes must keep a demonic king sealed by restoring a magical candle before time runs out, mixing dungeon crawling with town life and skill training. On the C64 it sat among late-80s Western CRPGs valued for atmosphere and systems depth beyond simple hack-and-slash.

The Misadventures of Flink.history: The Misadventures of Flink is a 1994 fantasy platformer by Fun Factory, published by Psygnosis for Amiga CD32 and Sega Mega Drive. Young wizard Flink gathers spells and creature allies across colourful side-scrolling stages. As a late Amiga-era Psygnosis platform title it showed the CD32 pushing cartoon action and magic-combo gameplay after the height of the OCS platform boom.

The New Zealand Story.history: Taito’s The New Zealand Story began in arcades in 1988; Ocean Software brought the cute kiwi rescue platformer to Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum. Floating balloons, whimsical enemies and demanding jumps defined its charm. Home ports kept a major Japanese arcade mascot title in European computer charts and remain favourites among Amiga and ST platform collectors.

The Pawn.history: The Pawn (1985–86) launched Magnetic Scrolls’ reputation, published by Rainbird with striking illustrations on Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and other machines. A witty fantasy text adventure in Kerovnia, it paired a sophisticated parser with optional graphics that showed off 16-bit displays. It helped make Rainbird adventures a prestige category on ST and Amiga shelves beside Infocom imports.

The Sacred Armour of Antiriad.history: Palace Software’s The Sacred Armour of Antiriad (1986) is a post-apocalyptic side-view adventure for Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and later 16-bit machines. Exploring ruins to recover a powered exosuit, players mix platforming with light inventory puzzles. On 8-bit micros it stood out for comic-book presentation and atmosphere, a stylish Palace title in the wake of Cauldron.

The Secret of Monkey Island.history: Lucasfilm Games’ The Secret of Monkey Island (1990) defined the comic point-and-click pirate adventure, with Amiga and Atari ST versions bringing Guybrush Threepwood’s quest to European 16-bit owners. Verb-based puzzles, insult sword fighting and Michael Land’s music made it a landmark. On Amiga especially it became a showcase adventure that set expectations for humour and production values in the early 1990s.

The Sentinel.history: Geoff Crammond’s The Sentinel (also known as The Sentry), published by Firebird in 1986, is an abstract 3D strategy-puzzle game for Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and later Amiga and Atari ST. Players absorb energy across barren landscapes while avoiding the gaze of a dominating Sentinel. Its tense, cerebral design felt unlike anything else on 8-bit machines and cemented Crammond’s reputation before his racing sims.

The Settlers.history: Blue Byte’s The Settlers (1993) is a landmark economic real-time strategy game for the Amiga, later ported elsewhere. Building roads, managing goods chains and expanding a medieval settlement created a living production network rather than pure military rush. On Amiga it became one of the defining early-90s strategy experiences and launched a franchise still associated with that serenely busy island-building fantasy.

The Seven Gates of Jambala.history: The Seven Gates of Jambala is a 1989 fantasy platform-adventure by Thalion Software, published by Grandslam for Amiga and Atari ST (with a later CD32 edition). A wizard seeks fragments of a magic wand through non-linear cave worlds full of shops, traps and tough enemies. An early Thalion release, it is remembered for mood, difficulty and soundtrack as part of the German studio’s first wave of 16-bit titles.

The Untouchables.history: Ocean Software’s The Untouchables (1989) adapts the Brian De Palma gangster film into multi-load action stages for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum. Players recreate set pieces from rooftop shootouts to the station shootout. Typical of Ocean’s late-80s movie licences, it mattered on European micros as a polished film tie-in that leaned on recognisable scenes rather than open sandbox crime play.

The Way of the Exploding Fist.history: Melbourne House’s The Way of the Exploding Fist (1985) brought one-on-one karate fighting to Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum, Amstrad CPC and other platforms. Fluid animations, multiple moves and versus play made it a breakout martial-arts hit before International Karate’s fame. On 8-bit machines it helped define the home-computer fighting-game boom and remains a landmark of mid-80s British software.

Thing on a Spring.history: Gremlin Graphics’ Thing on a Spring (1985) is a colourful platform-adventure for the Commodore 64 in which a toy-like spring creature explores a villain’s factory. Bouncy physics, collectibles and Rob Hubbard’s soundtrack made it a cheerful C64 favourite. It exemplified Gremlin’s mid-80s cute-action identity and still circulates widely among SID and platform fans.

Thrust.history: Thrust, designed by Jeremy Smith and published by Superior Software in 1986, is a physics-based cavern game for BBC Micro that spread to Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, Atari 8-bit and other systems. Piloting a rotate-and-thrust ship, players tow fuel pods out of gravity wells under hostile turrets. Its elegant controls and tension influenced later homebrew and indie physics flyers and became a cult classic of 8-bit design.

Thundercats.history: Elite Systems’ Thundercats (1987) is a side-scrolling action platformer based on the animated series, released for Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and related formats. Lion-O fights through stages toward Mumm-Ra in typical mid-80s licence fashion. On 8-bit machines it was one of several TV tie-ins that kept cartoon brands visible in computer shops during the merchandising peak of the decade.

Time Bandit.history: Time Bandit began on Atari 8-bit machines in the early 1980s and reached Amiga and Atari ST via Microdeal/MichTron as a top-down arcade adventure. Players warp through time gates into varied maze levels collecting treasures and keys. On 16-bit platforms its colourful multi-world structure and dual-player options made it a memorable early Microdeal action title bridging 8-bit arcade roots and ST/Amiga catalogues.

Times of Lore.history: Origin Systems’ Times of Lore (1988), designed by Chris Roberts, is a real-time action RPG for Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST, Amstrad CPC and other formats. A lone hero wanders a compact fantasy kingdom completing quests with direct arcade-like control rather than menu combat. It offered a more approachable Origin adventure beside Ultima and previewed Roberts’ interest in accessible real-time worlds.

Tiny Bobble.history: Tiny Bobble is a 2020 modern Amiga homebrew remake of Bubble Bobble by the demoscene group Abyss (code and audio by Pink). Built as a tiny single-file OCS/ECS executable, it aims closer to the arcade than the 1988 commercial Amiga port with 50 fps action, more colours and fuller animations. Clearly labelled freeware fan work, it became a showcase of how contemporary Amiga coders can outdo classic licensed conversions.

Toki.history: Toki (JuJu Densetsu) started as a 1989 TAD Corporation arcade platformer; Ocean Software published home versions for Amiga, Atari ST and other computers. An enchanted ape spits energy shots through jungle stages to reverse a curse. Bright humour and tough jumps made the Amiga/ST ports popular arcade conversions in Ocean’s early-90s line-up.

Total Eclipse.history: Incentive Software’s Total Eclipse (1988) uses the Freescape engine for a first-person pyramid adventure on Amstrad CPC, Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum and later 16-bit machines. Racing a cursed eclipse, players explore chambers, shoot doors and solve spatial puzzles in flat-shaded 3D. It proved Freescape could deliver atmospheric archaeology adventures on 8-bit hardware beyond Driller’s sci-fi debut.

Tower of Babel.history: Tower of Babel is a 1989 3D puzzle strategy game by Pete Cooke, published by Rainbird for Amiga, Atari ST and Commodore 64. Players coordinate specialised robots—such as grabbers and pushers—to collect crystals on interlocking towers under strict constraints. Cerebral and elegant, it stood out on 16-bit machines as a thoughtful Rainbird puzzler rather than an action showcase.

Trailblazer.history: Gremlin Graphics’ Trailblazer (1986) is a high-speed chequered-path racing game for Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum, Atari 8-bit and related systems. Bounce a ball along colour-coded panels that speed, slow or destroy you, alone or in split-screen. Its stark abstract look and relentless pace made it a distinctive mid-80s Gremlin hit and a favourite of two-player micro sessions.

Transarctica.history: Silmarils’ Transarctica (also known as Arctic Baron, 1993) is a post-apocalyptic strategy-adventure for Amiga, Atari ST and PC. Commanding an armed train across a frozen Earth, players trade, fight and hunt mammoths in a bid to restore the sun. On Amiga it exemplified French mid-90s ambition—bleak world-building mixed with management—typical of Silmarils’ atmospheric catalogue.

Transylvania.history: Transylvania is a classic illustrated adventure by Antonio Antiochia, first released by Penguin Software in 1982 and widely played on Apple II and Commodore 64 among other machines. Searching a gothic countryside for a king’s daughter, players parse puzzles amid wolves, castles and dark humour. It helped establish Penguin’s graphic-adventure style on 8-bit computers before later sequels continued the tale.

Trap.history: Trap is a 1986 vertical action game by Antony Crowther for Alligata Software on Commodore 64, with Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum versions. Stages mix space shooting, ground strafing and on-foot runs while Ben Daglish’s music drives the pace. A Crowther/Alligata showcase of the mid-80s C64 action scene, it is remembered as much for soundtrack and spectacle as for its multi-phase structure.

Treasure Island Dizzy.history: Treasure Island Dizzy (1988) continues the Codemasters egg-headed adventure series on Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 and later Amiga and Atari ST. Dizzy explores an island with inventory puzzles, hazards and the series’ infamous trial-and-error deaths. As an affordable Oliver twins hit it expanded Dizzy into a budget phenomenon across UK 8-bit machines and early 16-bit ports.

Turbo Out Run.history: Sega’s Turbo OutRun followed the arcade OutRun phenomenon in 1989; home ports by U.S. Gold and others reached Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum. Faster routes, weather and a pursuit turbo fantasy updated the coastal driving formula. On European micros it kept the OutRun brand alive as a demanding conversion centrepiece of the late 8- and 16-bit racing boom.

Turbo OutRun.history: Turbo OutRun, Sega’s 1989 arcade sequel to OutRun, arrived on Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and other home computers through U.S. Gold’s conversion programme. Players still race across stages in a Ferrari-style supercar, now with turbo boosts and tougher pacing. Computer versions could not match the cabinet’s power, yet they delivered the brand’s rush to living-room joysticks across Europe.

Turrican.history: Factor 5’s Turrican, published by Rainbow Arts in 1990, is a sprawling run-and-gun platformer for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and other formats. Huge non-linear levels, morph-ball style tricks and Chris Hülsbeck’s music created an arcade-quality epic on home computers. On Amiga and C64 especially it became a defining action showcase and launched one of Europe’s most beloved series.

Turrican 3.history: Turrican 3 (1993), developed by Factor 5 and published by Rainbow Arts for the Amiga, continues the series with larger weapons, bosses and polished set pieces (closely tied to Mega Turrican on consoles). Hülsbeck’s soundtrack and fluid blasting kept the franchise at the top of European action gaming. On late Amiga hardware it stood as a final 16-bit statement of the Turrican design language.

Turrican II.history: Turrican II: The Final Fight (1991) expanded Factor 5’s Rainbow Arts franchise on Amiga, Atari ST and Commodore 64 with vast maps, new weapons and iconic set pieces. Exploring, shooting and transforming through multi-stage worlds, it is widely ranked among the finest Amiga action games. Chris Hülsbeck’s score and technical polish made it a landmark of early-90s European software.

Turrican II - The Final Fight.history: Released in 1991 by Factor 5 and Rainbow Arts, Turrican II - The Final Fight pushed run-and-gun platforming on Amiga, Atari ST and Commodore 64 to new scale. Non-linear stages, inventive bosses and a celebrated soundtrack cemented the sequel’s reputation. For Amiga owners it became a must-own action epic and a high-water mark for what dedicated 16-bit coding teams could achieve.

Turrican II: The Final Fight.history: Turrican II: The Final Fight is Factor 5’s 1991 sequel published by Rainbow Arts across Amiga, Atari ST and Commodore 64.
