Bigger levels, richer firepower and unforgettable music built on the first game’s formula without losing exploration freedom. It mattered as a flagship European action title—often cited when arguing the Amiga’s best pure gameplay showcases of the early 1990s.

Turrican II: The Final Fight (2022).history: Turrican II: The Final Fight (2022) is a modern Amiga homebrew remake by Sonic Sloth, unofficial and freeware, based on the enhanced mid-90s PC DOS version and rebuilt for AGA machines. It restores effects, adds secrets and runs at full frame rate with richer colour. Clearly separate from Factor 5’s originals, it shows contemporary fans re-honing a classic for A1200-class hardware.

Tusker.history: System 3’s Tusker (1989) is an isometric action-adventure for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum. Set on an African expedition, players fight and explore toward ivory-poaching villains and lost secrets. Following The Last Ninja’s technical reputation, it extended System 3’s branded adventure style into a new setting for late-80s multicomputer audiences.

Twinworld - Land of Vision.history: TwinWorld: Land of Vision (1989) is a fantasy platform-adventure by Blue Byte, published by Ubi Soft for Amiga, Atari ST and Commodore 64. Young Ulric leaps through flip-screen worlds gathering magic to defeat the villain Carum. Cute presentation and solid 16-bit production made it an early Blue Byte credit before the studio’s strategy fame with The Settlers.

UFO: Enemy Unknown.history: UFO: Enemy Unknown (1994), known in North America as X-COM: UFO Defense, was developed by Mythos Games and published by MicroProse for Amiga and PC. Players fund a global defence force, research alien tech and fight turn-based tactical battles. On Amiga it became a defining strategy classic—punishing, systemic and hugely influential on later squad tactics games.

UFO: Enemy Unknown (AGA).history: The AGA Amiga edition of UFO: Enemy Unknown brings Mythos Games and MicroProse’s 1994 alien-invasion strategy to Amiga 1200-class machines with improved colour and performance headroom versus earlier chipsets. Geoscape management and grid tactics remain intact. For AGA owners it was the preferred way to play one of the platform’s essential early-90s strategy experiences.

UFO: Enemy Unknown (OCS/ECS).history: UFO: Enemy Unknown also shipped for OCS/ECS Amigas, delivering Mythos/MicroProse’s 1994 strategy blend of base building, research and turn-based battles on older chipsets. Though heavier than many A500 action titles, it still brought the full X-COM loop to a huge installed base. On classic Amigas it proved demanding sims could thrive beside platformers and shooters in the mid-90s library.

Ultima III: Exodus.history: Richard Garriott’s Ultima III: Exodus (1983), published by Origin Systems, advanced the series with party-based combat and a sharper moral-fantasy scope on Apple II, Commodore 64 and later Amiga and Atari ST among others. Players assemble heroes to confront Exodus across land and sea. On European micros it spread the Ultima tradition of open-world CRPGs that treated the computer as a living realm.

Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar.history: Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar (1985) shifted Origin’s series from demon-slaying to ethical virtue, asking players to become the Avatar through the Eight Virtues. Versions reached Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST and many other platforms. On home computers it was revolutionary—an RPG judged by honesty and compassion as much as combat—and remains a high point of 8- and 16-bit role-playing design.

Ultima V - Warriors of Destiny.history: Ultima V: Warriors of Destiny (1988) deepened Britannia with day-night cycles, denser NPC schedules and a story of tyranny twisting the Virtues. Origin’s release spanned Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST and other systems. On those machines it stood as a denser, darker sequel that rewarded patient exploration and cemented Ultima’s mid-series peak before the VGA-era shift.

Ultima V: Warriors of Destiny.history: Origin Systems released Ultima V: Warriors of Destiny in 1988 as a richer follow-up to the Avatar saga, with ports to Commodore 64, Amiga and Atari ST. Political oppression, detailed towns and tactical combat expanded the series’ simulation of daily life. For European 16-bit RPG fans it was a landmark of narrative ambition on disk-based home computers.

Ultima VI - The False Prophet.history: Ultima VI: The False Prophet (1990) rebuilt Origin’s series in a more continuous top-down world, widely played on PC and also on Amiga and Atari ST. Negotiating war between humans and gargoyles, it emphasised dialogue and cultural misunderstanding. On 16-bit machines it marked Ultima’s leap toward modern CRPG presentation while retaining Garriott’s virtue-driven storytelling.

Uninvited.history: ICOM Simulations’ Uninvited (1986) is a horror point-and-click adventure that began on Macintosh and reached Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and other platforms. Exploring a cursed mansion via windowed graphics and menu commands, players face sudden deaths and occult puzzles. With Déjà Vu, it helped define ICOM’s clickable Mac-adventure style on late-80s home computers.

Universe.history: Universe is a 1994 point-and-click adventure by Core Design for Amiga, CD32 and DOS. Originally conceived near Curse of Enchantia, it sends Boris Verne into a parallel space-opera realm to stop a tyrant. Rich colour and a serious tone made it Core’s late Amiga adventure statement before the studio shifted fully toward action—and later Tomb Raider—on newer platforms.

Unreal.history: Unreal is a 1990 Amiga action hybrid developed by Ordilogic Systems and published by Ubi Soft, with later Atari ST and MS-DOS ports. Across eight chapters it alternates pseudo-3D rail-shooter flights on a winged creature with side-scrolling barbarian platform stages. Magazines praised its detailed graphics and technical ambition beside titles like Shadow of the Beast, making it an early Ubisoft showcase of what 16-bit home machines could render in fantasy action.

Uridium.history: Uridium is Andrew Braybrook’s 1986 horizontally scrolling shoot-’em-up for Hewson on the Commodore 64, later ported to Amiga, Atari ST and other micros. Piloting a Manta fighter across vast dreadnought superstructures, it set a new bar for C64 smoothness, parallax presentation and arcade feel. It became one of the defining British 8-bit shmups and a landmark of Braybrook’s Graftgold-era craft before the Amiga sequel.

Uridium 2.history: Uridium 2 is Andrew Braybrook and Graftgold’s 1993 Amiga sequel to the C64 classic, published by Renegade. It rebuilds the dreadnought-skimming shooter formula with larger craft, heavier firepower and Amiga-era colour and sound. Arriving late in the commercial Amiga boom, it proved the original’s design still thrived on 16-bit hardware and remains a high-water mark for European home-computer shmups.

Utopia.history: Utopia (full title Utopia: The Creation of a Nation) is a 1991 real-time strategy and god-game hybrid by Celestial Software, published by Gremlin Graphics for Amiga and Atari ST, with later PC versions. Players colonise an alien world, balancing civilian growth, industry and military defence against rival colonists and native threats. It stood beside Populous and Mega-lo-Mania as a key early-’90s Amiga/ST management epic.

Utopia: The Creation of a Nation.history: Utopia: The Creation of a Nation is Celestial Software’s 1991 colony-building strategy game, published by Gremlin for Amiga, Atari ST and later PC. You expand a planetary settlement while managing resources, research and open warfare with competing factions. Its blend of city simulation and real-time conflict made it a standout Gremlin strategy title on 16-bit machines and a natural companion to the era’s god-game boom.

Victory Road.history: Victory Road (also known as Ikari Warriors II) is SNK’s 1986 arcade run-and-gun sequel, widely ported to Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST, Amstrad CPC and other homes. Two commandos blast through jungles and fortresses with grenades, tanks and co-op firepower in the classic Ikari mould. Home conversions kept the coin-op’s cooperative chaos in European living rooms when arcade shooters were a major computer-magazine draw.

Vindicator.history: The Vindicator! is a 1988 multi-stage action game developed by Ocean and published under the Imagine label for Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum and Amstrad CPC. After an underground maze hunt for alien blueprints, it switches to a vertical shooter stretch and a side-scrolling base assault. Typical of late-’80s Ocean multi-load epics, it brought varied arcade set-pieces and strong presentation to the British 8-bit catalogue.

Virocop.history: Virocop is a 1995 Amiga shoot-’em-up from Graftgold (Andrew Braybrook’s team), published by Renegade, with strong AGA support. You pilot antivirus craft through computer-themed stages, blasting viruses in a polished late-Amiga arcade package. One of the platform’s final commercial shmups from a classic British studio, it showed Graftgold still delivering slick action as the Amiga market narrowed.

Vroom.history: Vroom is a 1991 Formula One racing simulation by French studio Lankhor for Amiga and Atari ST. It emphasised fast 3D track rendering, realistic handling and Grand Prix presentation at a time when home computers competed hard in racing sims. Highly regarded in Europe for speed and feel, it helped prove Amiga and ST could host serious motorsport sims before later Geoff Crammond landmarks dominated the genre.

Vroom Multiplayer.history: Vroom Multiplayer extends Lankhor’s early-1990s Amiga/ST Formula One racer Vroom with head-to-head and shared racing options beyond the single-player Grand Prix campaign. Built on the same fast 3D engine that made the original a European favourite, it let friends race the same circuits together. On Amiga and Atari ST it underlined how local multiplayer turned already sharp racing sims into lasting living-room fixtures.

Walker.history: Walker is a 1993 Amiga action game by DMA Design, published by Psygnosis. You pilot a towering bipedal combat walker through horizontally scrolling war zones, stomping infantry and trading fire with armour and aircraft. With cinematic Psygnosis presentation and DMA’s trademark humour and punch, it became a memorable Amiga mech shooter and a bridge between the studio’s Lemmings fame and later console work.

War.history: W.A.R. (often listed simply as War) is a 1986 Commodore 64 horizontally scrolling shoot-’em-up published by Martech, with versions on other 8-bit machines. Players attack alien cylinder-worlds then crack colour-coded escape gates under time pressure. Remembered as much for Rob Hubbard’s celebrated SID soundtrack as for its Uridium-era blasting, it remains a fixture of C64 music and budget-to-full-price shooter history.

Warhawk.history: Warhawk is a 1986 vertically scrolling shoot-’em-up by Proteus Developments, released as a Firebird Silver budget title on Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, Atari 8-bit and later Atari ST. Cheap at £1.99 yet packed with relentless waves and a famous Rob Hubbard score, it punched far above its price. On the C64 especially, the music helped cement Warhawk as a cult SID classic as much as a Star Force-style blaster.

Wasteland.history: Wasteland is Interplay’s 1988 post-apocalyptic role-playing game, designed by Brian Fargo and team for Apple II, Commodore 64 and MS-DOS. Party-based squaddies explore a irradiated American Southwest with skill systems, branching consequences and dark humour. A landmark CRPG on late 8-bit and early PC platforms, it directly inspired Fallout and showed home computers could host ambitious, systemic narrative RPGs.

WEC Le Mans.history: WEC Le Mans is Konami’s 1986 arcade endurance racer, converted by Ocean for Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum. Drivers tackle the 24-hour Le Mans course with day-night cycles and demanding corners in a cockpit-style presentation. Ocean’s home ports brought a prestige coin-op racing licence to European micros when arcade conversions dominated the charts.

Wing Commander.history: Wing Commander is Origin Systems’ 1990 space combat simulation, created by Chris Roberts for MS-DOS PCs and later expanded across sequels and ports. Players fly as a Terran Confederation pilot in cinematic missions with wingmen, branching war outcomes and cutscene drama. It redefined PC space combat as a story-driven blockbuster and set expectations that Amiga and other platforms’ flight games were measured against through the early 1990s.

Wings.history: Wings is Cinemaware’s 1990 World War I flight game for the Amiga, later appearing on other systems. Between dogfights, bombing runs and journal-style campaign narrative, it cast the player as a rookie pilot on the Western Front. Lavish for its day and tightly tuned to Amiga hardware, it remains one of Cinemaware’s best-loved titles and a high point of interactive storytelling on 16-bit machines.

Wings of Death.history: Wings of Death is a 1990 fantasy shoot-’em-up by Eclipse Software, published by Thalion for Amiga and Atari ST. A mage transforms into winged forms to blast through vertically scrolling stages packed with bosses and power-ups. With strong European demo-scene pedigree and a memorable soundtrack, it became a flagship Thalion shmup and a staple of Amiga/ST arcade collections.

Winter Games.history: Winter Games is Epyx’s 1985 multi-event winter sports title, a sequel-style follow-up to Summer Games on Commodore 64 and widely ported to Amiga, Atari ST, Amstrad CPC and other platforms. Hot-seat Olympic events from skiing to skating emphasised timing and joystick skill. Part of Epyx’s defining Games series, it helped make multi-sport party compilations a core genre on 8- and 16-bit home computers.

Wizball.history: Wizball is Sensible Software’s 1987 colour-restoration shoot-’em-up, published by Ocean on Commodore 64 and later Amiga, Atari ST and other micros. As a bouncing wizard ball you collect pigments to repaint a drained world, mixing odd controls with sharp shooting. Martin Galway’s C64 score became one of the most celebrated SIDs ever, and the game’s originality made it a lasting Sensible/Ocean classic.

Wizkid.history: Wizkid: The Story of Wizball II is Sensible Software’s 1992 Amiga puzzle-platform follow-up to Wizball, published by Psygnosis. A floating wizard kid batters enemies to free cats and solve surreal screen puzzles with Sensible’s trademark humour. Quirky design and Psygnosis presentation made it a cult late Amiga original from the team behind Wizball and Cannon Fodder.

World Circuit.history: World Circuit is the North American title of Geoff Crammond’s Formula One Grand Prix (1991), published by MicroProse for Amiga, Atari ST and PC. It delivered a full F1 season with detailed handling, authentic circuits and deep options that set a new realism bar. On Amiga and ST it became the definitive early-’90s Grand Prix sim and the foundation for Crammond’s later Grand Prix series.

World Class Leader Board.history: World Class Leader Board is Access Software’s mid-to-late 1980s golf simulation, expanding the Leader Board series onto Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST and other platforms. Multiple famous courses, wind and precise swing control made it a sports-sim staple. On home computers it helped establish golf as a serious simulation genre rather than a simple arcade diversion.

World Games.history: World Games is Epyx’s 1986 multi-sport follow-up to Summer and Winter Games, released on Commodore 64 and widely ported to Amiga, Atari ST, CPC and more. Events drawn from around the globe—log rolling, bull riding, cliff diving—kept the joystick-skill party format fresh. It extended Epyx’s Games franchise that defined multi-event sports compilations on 8- and 16-bit machines.

World Karate Championship.history: World Karate Championship is the U.S. title for System 3’s International Karate (1985–86), published by Epyx on Commodore 64 and other platforms. One-on-one tournament fighting across global backdrops emphasised timing and readable moves years before Street Fighter II. Rob Hubbard’s music and sharp C64 animation made it a foundational Western fighting game on home computers.

Worms.history: Worms is Team17’s 1995 turn-based artillery strategy game that began on Amiga before exploding onto PCs and consoles. Squads of cartoon worms lob grenades, bazookas and absurd weapons across destructible 2D landscapes. Born from Andy Davidson’s Amiga digger concept Blitz, it became one of the Amiga’s last global hits and a long-running multiplayer franchise.

Worms (AGA).history: Worms (AGA) is the Enhanced Amiga version of Team17’s 1995 artillery classic, tuned for Advanced Graphics Architecture machines such as the A1200. It keeps the turn-based worm warfare, destructible terrain and comic weapon set while taking advantage of AGA colour and performance. For many Amiga owners it was the definitive way to play the original hit that launched a multi-platform series.

Worms: The Director's Cut.history: Worms: The Director’s Cut is Team17’s 1997 Amiga-exclusive expansion of the original Worms, adding new weapons, missions and editor tools beyond the 1995 game. Built for late Amiga hardware, it was a love letter to the platform that launched the series. Still prized by Amiga fans, it stands as one of the machine’s last major commercial exclusives of the 1990s.

Worthy.history: Worthy is a modern commercial Amiga homebrew maze-action game by Pixelglass Games, released in 2018 for OCS/ECS Amigas and CD32. Guide prince Aldo through dozens of trap-filled levels collecting diamonds to prove himself, with 32-colour pixel art and original music. Clearly labelled as a contemporary release for classic hardware, it showed the Amiga scene could still ship polished boxed and digital games decades after the commercial peak.

X-Out.history: X-Out is a 1989–1990 underwater horizontal shoot-’em-up by Arc Developments, published by Rainbow Arts for Amiga, Atari ST and other systems. Players buy weapons and modules then dive through scrolling alien seas toward large end-of-level threats. Part of Rainbow Arts’ strong European shmup line, it paired shop-based upgrades with slick 16-bit presentation and led directly to the sequel Z-Out.

Xenon.history: Xenon is the Bitmap Brothers’ debut shoot-’em-up, released in 1988 by Melbourne House / Image Works for Amiga and Atari ST, with later ports. Alternating airborne and ground-transforming craft through vertical stages, it announced the studio’s glossy metallic visual style. A breakthrough UK 16-bit arcade title, it paved the way for Xenon 2 and the Bitmap Brothers’ run of Amiga/ST hits.

Xenon 2: Megablast.history: Xenon 2: Megablast is the Bitmap Brothers’ 1989 Amiga and Atari ST sequel to Xenon, published by Image Works, with console and PC versions following. A vertically scrolling blaster with shop upgrades and huge bosses, it was famous for licensing Bomb the Bass’s Megablast as its theme. Stylish graphics and chart-ready music made it one of the defining late-’80s 16-bit shmups.

Xenon II - Megablast.history: Xenon II – Megablast (also styled Xenon 2: Megablast) is the Bitmap Brothers’ 1989 sequel published by Image Works on Amiga, Atari ST and beyond. It refines the vertical shooter formula with power purchases, dense enemy waves and the licensed Bomb the Bass title track. On European 16-bit machines it became a showcase of how coin-op intensity and pop-crossover audio could sell home-computer arcade games.

Xyphoes Fantasy.history: Xyphoes Fantasy is a late-1980s French role-playing adventure by Silmarils, released on Amstrad CPC and later Amiga and Atari ST. Players explore a fantasy world through icon-driven interaction, combat and character progression typical of Silmarils’ early CRPGs. It helped establish the studio’s reputation on francophone micros before Ishar and other larger Amiga/ST RPGs.

Yie Ar Kung-Fu.history: Yie Ar Kung-Fu is Konami’s 1985 arcade one-on-one fighter, widely converted by Imagine/Ocean to Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and other homes. Challengers face a gauntlet of martial artists with distinct weapons and patterns. Martin Galway’s C64 audio and the game’s clear one-on-one structure made it an early fighting-game staple on European 8-bit computers.

Yo! Joe!.history: Yo! Joe! is a 1993 Amiga platformer developed by Scipio and published by Play Byte (with later CD32 attention). Two leather-jacketed heroes punch and jump through colourful cartoon stages in a slick co-op-friendly beat-’em-up platform style. Often cited as a late Amiga exclusive gem, it showed European developers still delivering console-smooth platform action on Commodore hardware.

Z-Out.history: Z-Out is Rainbow Arts’ 1990 sequel to X-Out, developed for Amiga and Atari ST as a horizontally scrolling shoot-’em-up. Players again kit out a craft and fight through dense underwater and alien stages with large bosses. Building on its predecessor’s shop-and-blast loop, it ranked among the stronger European 16-bit shmups of the Rainbow Arts catalogue.

Zak McKracken and the Alien Mindbenders.history: Zak McKracken and the Alien Mindbenders is Lucasfilm Games’ 1988 graphic adventure, built with the SCUMM engine for Commodore 64, Amiga, Atari ST, PC and later FM Towns. Tabloid reporter Zak and allies foil an alien plot to dumb down humanity through surreal globe-spanning puzzles. Following Maniac Mansion, it cemented Lucasfilm’s adventure style on 8- and 16-bit platforms.

Zamzara.history: Zamzara is a 1988 Commodore 64 shoot-’em-up by Frantic Software, published by Hewson, with music by Charles Deenen of Maniacs of Noise. A bio-engineered warrior blasts through horizontally scrolling alien threats in a polished late-’80s C64 package. Deenen’s SID work helped push the game into HVSC favourites, keeping Zamzara alive in C64 music culture as well as shooter retrospectives.

Zoids.history: Zoids is a 1986 strategy-action game by Paul Shirley, published by Martech on Commodore 64 and ZX Spectrum, based on the mechanical-beast toy line. Players manage resources and combat to reclaim a planet from rival Zoid forces in a tense, systems-heavy campaign. Rob Hubbard’s soundtrack became a SID classic, and the game stood out as an unusually deep licensed title on British 8-bit machines.

Zombi.history: Zombi is Ubisoft’s late-1980s survival horror adventure inspired by Dawn of the Dead, released on Amiga, Atari ST, Amstrad CPC and other micros. Players scavenge a zombie-infested shopping mall, managing inventory and escape while tension builds screen by screen. An early Ubisoft horror outing on European home computers, it prefigured later mall-siege zombie games with stark pixel atmosphere.

Zool.history: Zool is Gremlin Graphics’ 1992 Amiga platformer starring a “ninth-century ninja ant,” positioned as Commodore’s answer to Sonic-era mascot games. High-speed stages, smart bombs and candy-coloured worlds showed off Amiga smoothness and became a CD32 pack-in highlight. Zool turned into a short-lived but iconic Amiga mascot franchise and a defining early-’90s Gremlin hit.

Zool 2.history: Zool 2 is Gremlin’s 1993 sequel to the Amiga mascot platformer Zool, also appearing on other platforms including CD32. The ninja ant returns with new moves, companion Mental Marty and denser, faster levels aimed at the console-platformer crowd. It extended Gremlin’s push to keep Amiga platform games competitive during the early 1990s console boom.

Zub.history: Zub is a 1986 budget platform-adventure by Binary Design, published by Mastertronic on Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum and Amstrad CPC. An alien messenger hops between planets via teleport pads, dodging hazards to deliver a vital message. Cheap, colourful and accessible, it exemplified Mastertronic’s high-volume 8-bit budget scene that filled European software charts.

Zynaps.history: Zynaps is a 1987 horizontally scrolling shoot-’em-up by John Cumming and Dominic Robinson for Hewson, launched on ZX Spectrum and Commodore 64 with later Amiga and Atari ST versions. Gradual weapon upgrades and tough arcade pacing earned strong reviews on British micros. It joined Uridium and Exolon in Hewson’s late-’80s reputation for sharp, no-nonsense home-computer blasters.

Advantage Tennis.history: Advantage Tennis is a 1991 tennis video game developed and published by Infogrames for the Amiga, Atari ST, and MS-DOS.

The Adventures of Robin Hood.history: The Adventures of Robin Hood is a video game released in the autumn of 1991 by Millennium Interactive.
The Adventures of Robin Hood.page: The Adventures of Robin Hood (video game)

Barbarian 2.history: Barbarian II: The Dungeon of Drax is a video game first published in 1988 for various home computers. It was released as Axe of Rage in North America. The game is the sequel to Barbarian: The Ultimate Warrior (Death Sword in North America), which was published in 1987. In Barbarian II, the player controls a princess or barbarian character, exploring the game world to locate and defeat an evil wizard. The game's plot is an extension of its predecessor, although the gameplay is different. While the first game offers two players the opportunity for virtual head-to-head combat, the second is a single-player beat 'em up with fewer fighting moves. It uses a flip-screen style instead of scrolling. Palace Software, the developer of the two Barbarian games, marketed the sequel with the same strategy they used for the first game. They hired Maria Whittaker, a model known for her topless work, to pose on the cover and posters as the princess in the game, attempting to recapture the controversy that had boosted sales. Barbarian II received a mixed critical reception.

Battle Isle.history: Battle Isle is a 1991 turn-based strategy video game developed by Blue Byte and published by Ubi Soft for the Amiga and MS-DOS. It is the first game in the Battle Isle series. Two official expansion packs were released: Data Disk I in 1992 and The Moon of Chromos in 1993. An unofficial expansion, Battle Field Creator, was released in 1994. An Atari ST version was advertised but never released.

Black Crypt.history: Black Crypt is a role-playing video game for the Amiga published by Electronic Arts in 1992. It was Raven Software's debut title. Its 3D realtime style is similar to FTL Games' popular Dungeon Master, where the player leads a party of four heroes through a large dungeon to ultimately confront and defeat a powerful enemy. A version for the Mega Drive was in development, but never released.

Dark Seed.history: Dark Seed is a psychological horror point-and-click adventure game developed and published by Cyberdreams in 1992. It is set in a normal world and a dark world counterpart, the latter based on artwork by H. R. Giger. It was one of the first point-and-click adventure games to use high-resolution (640 × 350 pixels) graphics, to Giger's demand. A sequel, Dark Seed II, was released in 1995.

Desert Strike.history: Desert Strike: Return to the Gulf is a shoot 'em up video game released by Electronic Arts (EA) in 1992 for the Sega Genesis. The game was released on several other formats such as the Super Nintendo Entertainment System, including a much upgraded version for the Amiga home computer. The game was inspired by the Gulf War and depicts a conflict between an insane Middle Eastern dictator, General Kilbaba, and the United States. The player controls an Apache helicopter and attempts to destroy enemy weapons and installations, rescue hostages and capture enemy personnel, while managing supplies of fuel and ammunition. Lead designer Mike Posehn had no video game experience prior to developing Desert Strike. Inspired by Choplifter, he aimed to create a nonlinear game with smoothly animated vehicles. Posehn developed a camera system with momentum to mimic realistic helicopter movements. Three-dimensional (3D) modeling was used to generate the vehicle sprites, which were later touched up on the pixel level with color. Desert Strike was a commercial success: it was a chart-topping best seller and at the time Electronics Arts' highest selling game. The game also received a favourable critical response, with several magazines awarding scores of over 90%.

Drakkhen.history: Drakkhen is a 1989 3D role-playing video game, initially developed and published by Infogrames for the Amiga and Atari ST, and ported to MS-DOS, Super NES, PC-98, X68000, and FM Towns Marty. It was a very early game in the North American SNES library, and as such, received almost universal coverage in previews of the then-upcoming SNES in gaming magazines of 1990 and early 1991. Drakkhen was among the first role-playing games with a three-dimensional playing field and an early example of the real-time tactics genre. It did not employ a fully 3D game engine, instead implementing a hybrid approach using vectors and bitmapped character-scaling algorithms. Drakkhen includes an animated day-night cycle and the ability to wander freely about the game world, both rarities for a game of its era. The game spawned a Super NES sequel: Dragon View.

Extase.history: Extase is a computer game developed by Cryo and published by Virgin Mastertronic.

F/A-18 Interceptor.history: F/A-18 Interceptor is a combat flight simulator developed by Intellisoft and published by Electronic Arts for the Amiga in 1988. The player mainly flies the F/A-18 Hornet, but the F-16 Fighting Falcon is also available for aerobatics, free flight and the first mission. Contrary to the title of the game, the real F/A-18 is not a true interceptor aircraft, having been designed instead as a multirole anti-ship strike fighter.

Faery Tale Adventure, The.history: The Faery Tale Adventure is a 1987 action role-playing video game designed by David Joiner and published by MicroIllusions for the Amiga, and later ported to the Commodore 64, MS-DOS, and Sega Genesis. The MS-DOS version is titled The Faery Tale Adventure: Book I. Microillusions also released a "Book 1" version for the Amiga which was going to be the start of a series of games, according to Talin, but bankruptcy prevented it. The initial version was produced for the Amiga 1000 and featured the largest game world to that date. A sequel, Faery Tale Adventure II: Halls of the Dead, was released in 1997.

Flood.history: Flood is a 1990 platform game developed by Bullfrog Productions. It was published for the Amiga and Atari ST by Electronic Arts. The objective is to collect all the litter and find the exit to the level.

The Godfather.history: The Godfather is a side-scrolling run and gun video game released by U.S. Gold in 1991 for the Amiga, Atari ST, and MS-DOS. A Master System version was cancelled. The plot is based on the three Godfather films. There are five levels which reflect the locations seen in the movies, including the streets of New York City, Miami, and the village of Corleone in Sicily.

Heimdall.history: Heimdall is an action role-playing game developed by The 8th Day, published by Core Design, and released in 1991 for the Amiga and for the Atari ST and MS-DOS in 1992. A Mega-CD version was published in early 1994. The game is a mixture of puzzle-solving, exploration, and dynamic combat mechanics, where players must explore various islands in the search for the fabled weapons belonging to the gods of Norse mythology. The game received favourable reviews upon its release, except for the Mega-CD which received mixed feedback. A sequel, Heimdall 2, was developed by the same group and released three years later in 1994.

Marble Madness.history: Marble Madness is a 1984 platform game designed by Mark Cerny and published by Atari Games Inc. for arcades. Set in an isometric perspective, the game tasks the player with guiding a marble through six courses, populated with obstacles and enemies, within a time limit. The player controls the marble by using a trackball. Marble Madness is known for using innovative game technologies: it was Atari's first to use the Atari System 1 hardware, the first to be programmed in the C programming language, and one of the first to use true stereo sound (previous games used either monaural sound or simulated stereo). In designing the game, Cerny drew inspiration from miniature golf, racing games, and the art of M. C. Escher. He aimed to create a game that offered a distinct experience with a unique control system. Cerny applied a minimalist approach in designing the appearance of the game's courses and enemies. Throughout development, he was frequently impeded by limitations in technology and had to forgo several design ideas. Upon its release in arcades, Marble Madness was commercially successful and profitable. Critics praised the game's difficulty, unique visual design, and stereo soundtrack.

Maupiti Island.history: Maupiti Island is a point-and-click adventure game developed and published by Lankhor. It was released in 1990 and is the sequel to Mortville Manor. The player controls Jérôme Lange, a detective attempting to solve a crime by interacting with various characters and collecting clues while further events unveil a complex plot.

Operation Stealth.history: Operation Stealth, also known as 007 James Bond: The Stealth Affair in the United States, is a 1990 adventure game from Delphine Software International. The game is mainly the work of Paul Cuisset (programming) and Jean Baudlot (sound). The game was released with the Bond license in the United States, although this led to some inconsistencies as the MI6 agent appeared to be taking his orders from the CIA.

Putty.history: Putty (also known as Silly Putty or Look Out It's...Putty) is a game developed by System 3 and released in 1992 for the Amiga. It was also released on the Super Nintendo Entertainment System in 1993 as Super Putty (Putty Moon (パティームーン, Patī Mūn) in Japan) and Amiga CD32 version was published in 1994 under the same name.

Robocop 3.history: RoboCop 3 is a video game based on the 1993 film of the same name. Amiga, Atari ST, and MS-DOS versions were developed by Digital Image Design and published by Ocean Software in December 1991. The Digital Image Design version includes multiple gameplay styles. During 1992 and 1993, other versions consisting of side-scrolling platform gameplay were released for the Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum, NES, Super NES, Game Gear, Master System, and Genesis.

Ruff 'n' Tumble.history: Ruff 'n' Tumble is a 1994 platform run and gun video game developed by Wunderkind and published by Renegade Software for the Amiga. An Amiga CD32 version was planned but never released. It was the only game made by Wunderkind. It stars Ruff Rodgers, embarking on a quest across an alien planet to reclaim his marbles after one of them fell into a portal inside a rabbit hole while playing with his collection in the park, and free the planet from Dr. Destiny and his Tinhead army. Through the journey, the player explores and search through each level for items and power-ups, as well as fight enemies and defeat bosses. Ruff 'n' Tumble was the creation of Wunderkind, a group within Renegade consisting of programmer Jason Perkins, artist Robin Levy, and composer Jason Page. Levy was contacted by Perkins, due to their previous working experience on Apocalypse (1994) for Virgin Interactive Entertainment, and was asked if he was interested in making a game with him. Perkins wanted to make a platform game while Levy preferred a shoot 'em up, with the original idea being a "platform-based Defender".

Soccer Kid.history: Soccer Kid is a 1993 side-scrolling platform game developed and published by Krisalis Software in Europe for the Amiga. The player assumes the role of the titular main protagonist who travels across several countries around the world to repair the World Cup by retrieving pieces that were scattered by the alien pirate Scab, the main antagonist who failed to steal and add it to his trophy collection in a robbery attempt. Its gameplay mainly consists of platforming and exploration elements, with a main single-button or two-button configuration, depending on the controls setup. Conceived by Dean Lester, Soccer Kid was created by most of the same team who previously worked on the Manchester United franchise at Krisalis Software and uses the same game engine as with Arabian Nights, another title made by the developer. After making multiple association football titles, the team experimented with creating a project that fused both football and platform game elements in 1992, developing a physics engine dedicated to the soccer ball that proved to be successful internally.

Croisière pour un Cadavre.history: Cruise for a Corpse (orig. Croisière pour un cadavre) is an adventure game from Delphine Software International, made for the Amiga, Atari ST, and MS-DOS.

Great Courts 2.history: Pro Tennis Tour 2 (published as Great Courts 2 in France and Germany, and Jimmy Connors Pro Tennis Tour in North America) is a sports video game developed by Blue Byte Software for the Amiga and published by Ubi Soft in 1991. It is the sequel to the 1989 game Pro Tennis Tour (also released as Great Courts). Pro Tennis Tour 2 was ported to MS-DOS compatible operating systems and the Atari ST. A sequel, Jimmy Connors Pro Tennis Tour (1992), was released for the Super Nintendo.

Teenage Queen.history: Teenage Queen is a late-1980s erotic card game from French studio ERE Informatique (Infogrames), released on Amiga, Atari ST and related micros. Players advance through strip-poker style rounds against a single computer opponent, with illustrated reveals typical of the era’s adult leisure titles on home computers. Light on rules and heavy on presentation, it sat at the fringe of the Amiga leisure catalogue—more novelty diversion than competitive card sim—and remains a period curiosity from the French software scene that also produced more ambitious adventures and action games.

Les Voyageurs du Temps.history: Future Wars, subtitled in Europe as Time Travellers and in North America as Adventures in Time, and known in France as Time Travellers: The Menace (French: Les Voyageurs du Temps: La Menace), is an adventure game from Delphine Software International, released in 1989. The game is mainly the work of Paul Cuisset (story and programming) and Éric Chahi (graphics). The game was intended to be the first of a series of adventure games revolving around time travelling but later episodes were never made.
